info.title: Proteles Management API
info.description:
The control plane: tenants, applications, connections, users, webhooks and the audit trail.

This document is checked against the server's own route table on every pipeline, so a route added without a corresponding operation here fails CI.

**Two conditions apply to every operation and are not repeated on each one.** A 429 can refuse any call: the limiter meters `/api/v1/` by prefix, not from a list of routes. And when the Management API is disabled for the deployment, every operation answers **404** `not_found` ("the management API is disabled") rather than 401 or 503 — the surface is meant to be indistinguishable from one that was never mounted. A 404 is therefore not always a missing resource, and a client that reads it as one will report a deployment-wide outage as fifty missing records.

get.summary: Monthly recurring users, now and over time
get.description:
What this tenant is consuming, and useful before any
pricing exists: "how much is this tenant using" is a question an operator has
today and could previously answer only with hand-written SQL over the audit log.

The number's definition travels with it in every response. A bare `active_users`
invites the reader to supply their own — rolling thirty days, sign-ins only, per
application — and each of those is a different figure. An invoice dispute is a
bad place to discover which one was meant.

`active_users` is the last point of `series` by construction, read from one query
rather than two, so the headline and the chart cannot disagree across a month
boundary.
get.x-auth:
auth.tenant_scope(q.tenant_id)
auth.require_scope(SCOPE_USAGE_READ)   // "usage:read" — STRICT

Strict, and for a narrower reason than the other strict scopes: this is not a
credential and reading it takes nothing over. It is the tenant's commercial
position — how many customers they have and how fast that is changing — which is
not something an unscoped integration key should acquire by default.

There is deliberately no `usage:write`. These numbers are recorded by the act of
somebody signing in, and an endpoint that could adjust them would be an endpoint
that could adjust an invoice.

parameters.name: tenant_id
parameters.description: Required with the platform token; refused if it names a tenant other than a tenant key's own.

parameters.name: months
parameters.description: How many calendar months of history, ending with the current one. Default 12, clamped to 24 — an unbounded value would let one low-privilege key make the database generate an arbitrarily long series. `0` is read as the default rather than as an empty series, which is more likely a caller bug than an intention.

200.description: The current month's figure and the requested history.

400.description: `invalid_request` — "tenant_id is required when using the platform token".

404.description: `not_found` — the Management API is disabled on this deployment.

get.summary: The operational numbers that live in Postgres
get.description:
Webhook queue depth, unacknowledged dead letters, audit export lag in seals, and
audit rows no seal covers. Each is a silent failure: the first symptom of any of
them is somebody asking why an integration went quiet, or an auditor asking for a
range that was never attested.

These were reachable only through `/metrics`, which sits behind `METRICS_TOKEN`,
outside tenant resolution, and is shaped for a scraper. Prometheus could graph
them; the person on call with a browser could not see them at all.

Reuses the same cached, bounded read the scrape uses — a 2s ceiling and a 10s
floor — so a second reader cannot double the aggregate queries, and a struggling
database cannot hold up the page somebody opened *because* it is struggling.
get.x-auth:
auth.require_platform()

Platform only, because these are fleet-wide: the query carries no tenant
predicate, so a tenant reading it would learn how much traffic every other tenant
is generating. There is deliberately no per-tenant version — a tenant's own dead
letters are already at /api/v1/webhook/dead-letters, scoped like everything else.

200.description: The four numbers, as of at most ten seconds ago.

503.description:
`unavailable` — the numbers could not be read from the database.
Deliberately not a 200 carrying zeros: "queue depth 0" during an outage reads
as healthy, and it is the number an operator would most like to trust. An
explicit refusal is the honest answer.

get.summary: Where this tenant's mail goes out from
get.description:
Reads the tenant's SMTP relay, or reports that it uses the platform default.

The password is never returned in any form. A tenant with no configuration is answered
200 with `configured: false` and the name of the fallback, not 404 — "this tenant uses
the platform relay" is an answer about a working system, and a 404 reads as "mail is
broken" to anyone who does not already know the difference.
get.x-auth:
auth.tenant_scope(q.tenant_id)
auth.require_scope(SCOPE_MAIL_READ)   // "mail:read" — STRICT

Strict, unlike the older read scopes: a key that declared no scopes at all does NOT
acquire it. `mail:read` and `mail:write` ship after scope enforcement, so no key minted
before them has ever been able to use them — the same asymmetry as `domains:write`
(management.rs) — and the stored host and username are a map of the tenant's mail
infrastructure.

parameters.name: tenant_id
parameters.description: Required with the platform token; refused if it names a tenant other than a tenant key's own.

200.description: The relay, or the platform fallback.

400.description: `invalid_request` — "tenant_id is required when using the platform token".

404.description: `not_found` — the Management API is disabled on this deployment.

put.description:
Writes the tenant's SMTP settings, replacing any that were there.

Refused before anything is stored: an unknown `encryption` name, a `from_address` that is
not an address, a password with no username (SMTP AUTH has no such shape), and
unencrypted SMTP to anything but loopback. The last is the one worth stating — cleartext
SMTP off-box puts the password *and every reset link* on the network in the clear.

The configuration is also *built* as a transport before storing, so one the sender cannot
use is a 400 rather than a saved setting that fails at 3am on somebody's password reset.

The delivery-outcome fields survive an edit. Renaming the From: line has not un-sent
yesterday's mail, and clearing them would tell an operator their working relay had never
sent anything.
put.x-auth:
auth.tenant_scope(req.tenant_id)
auth.require_scope(SCOPE_MAIL_WRITE)   // "mail:write" — STRICT

The strictest thing in this group, and the reason both scopes are strict: whoever can
write these settings can point the relay at a host they control, and every password-reset
link this tenant sends then arrives in their inbox. "Forgot password" becomes a way of
collecting accounts, with no step that looks unusual to the user.

parameters.name: X-Proteles-Operator
parameters.description: Asserted operator for the `mail.settings_updated`, `mail.settings_deleted` and `mail.test_sent` audit rows, recorded in `detail` as `asserted_operator=`. Only the server writes that key: an `asserted_operator=` arriving inside any other caller-supplied text is neutralised, so it cannot pose as an attribution. Platform token only; ignored for a tenant key.

200.description: Stored, and read back. Audited as `mail.settings_updated` at **warning** severity with the host in `detail` — the question an incident asks is *where was it pointed, and when*.

400.description: `invalid_request` — "invalid JSON body", "encryption must be one of starttls, implicit, none", "host is required", "port must be between 1 and 65535", "from_address must be an email address", "a password needs a username", "unencrypted SMTP is only allowed to localhost…", or a message from the transport builder (an address the mail transport refuses, a host the TLS layer will not accept as a server name).

404.description: `not_found` — the Management API is disabled on this deployment.

delete.summary: Fall back to the platform relay
delete.description: Removes the tenant's settings. Its mail then goes out through the platform default.

parameters.name: tenant_id
parameters.description: Required with the platform token; refused if it names a tenant other than a tenant key's own.

parameters.name: X-Proteles-Operator
parameters.description: Asserted operator for the `mail.settings_updated`, `mail.settings_deleted` and `mail.test_sent` audit rows, recorded in `detail` as `asserted_operator=`. Only the server writes that key: an `asserted_operator=` arriving inside any other caller-supplied text is neutralised, so it cannot pose as an attribution. Platform token only; ignored for a tenant key.

204.description: Removed. Audited as `mail.settings_deleted` at warning severity — moving mail back to the platform relay is a move too.

400.description: `invalid_request` — "tenant_id is required when using the platform token".

404.description: `not_found` — "this tenant has no mail settings". A second delete is a 404 rather than a cheerful 204: an operator who expected to remove something should hear that they did not. Also `not_found` when the Management API is disabled.

post.summary: Send a test message through the stored configuration
post.description:
Most of the point of the admin surface. Without it, the way an operator finds out their
SMTP settings are wrong is that a user cannot get back into their account — both the worst
time to discover it and the hardest to attribute.

It sends through the **stored** configuration, not one supplied in the body: testing
something other than what will be used is a test that can pass while the real thing is
broken. Save, then test.

A relay that refuses answers **200** with `sent: false` and the relay's own message. See
`MailTestResult`.
post.x-auth:
auth.tenant_scope(req.tenant_id)
auth.require_scope(SCOPE_MAIL_WRITE)   // "mail:write", not mail:read

Write rather than read, deliberately: this sends real mail, to an address the caller
chooses, from this tenant's domain. That is a capability, not an inspection.

parameters.name: X-Proteles-Operator
parameters.description: Asserted operator for the `mail.settings_updated`, `mail.settings_deleted` and `mail.test_sent` audit rows, recorded in `detail` as `asserted_operator=`. Only the server writes that key: an `asserted_operator=` arriving inside any other caller-supplied text is neutralised, so it cannot pose as an attribution. Platform token only; ignored for a tenant key.

200.description: The attempt was made. `sent` says whether the relay took it. Audited as `mail.test_sent` at info severity with the recipient and the outcome — a burst of failures is an operator fixing a relay, and a burst of successes to varying addresses is somebody using this endpoint to send mail from the tenant's domain.

400.description: `invalid_request` — "invalid JSON body" (also the answer when `to` is absent, since the field is required), "a recipient address is required" (`to` blank once trimmed), or "to must be an email address" (`to` is not a bare address at a host name; see the request schema).

404.description: `not_found` — the Management API is disabled on this deployment.

post.summary: Provision an OAuth client (an "app") in a tenant
post.description:
The operator's way to create a client. Distinct from RFC 7591
self-registration at `POST /register` in three ways that matter:

* The created client gets **no registration access token**, so it is
  managed here and nowhere else — "handing it a self-management
  credential would mean anyone who obtained that token could rewrite an
  app the operator created".
* It is therefore not *self-registered*, so it neither counts against nor
  is refused by the per-tenant registration quota: "squatters filling a
  tenant would lock its operator out of provisioning the very client
  needed to fix it".
* It cannot be deleted by `DELETE /api/v1/apps/{client_id}`, which
  reaches self-registered rows only.

Three properties are server-set and not expressible in the request body:
`require_pkce` is always `true`, `logo_uri` is always null, and
`is_active` is always `true`.

With a tenant's own key, the tenant is held to its plan version's
application limit where plans are enforced: at the limit,
403 `limit_reached`, and nothing already created is removed. The platform
token is not held to it.
post.x-auth:
auth.tenant_scope(req.tenant_id)                        // :753
auth.require_scope_if_restricted(SCOPE_APPS_WRITE)      // :757  ("apps:write")

parameters.name: X-Proteles-Operator
parameters.description:
Who the caller says is acting, recorded beside the credential in the
audit row. A header and never a body
field, because "a body field is reachable from a form post in a way a
custom header is not". HONOURED ONLY FOR THE PLATFORM TOKEN: a tenant
key that sends it has it ignored and warn-logged, not refused, since
"turning a stray header from a reverse proxy into a 403 would make an
attribution feature into an outage". Charset is 1-256
bytes of `[A-Za-z0-9._\-@+:%]` — no whitespace, no `=`, no control
characters, because the value is interpolated into a `k=v` audit
detail. A value outside that set, or the
header sent twice, is recorded as the sentinel `(rejected)` rather
than dropped; it never fails the request.

requestBody.description:
A body is required in practice: a missing or unreadable one is a 400
`invalid_request` ("invalid JSON body") rather than a default. A missing
`content-type: application/json` gets that same answer, and so does an
unknown field — as it does on API-key creation — so `{"name": ...}` is
refused rather than creating a client named after its own `client_id`.

201.description:
Created. `client_secret` is present only for a confidential client —
that is, when `token_endpoint_auth_method` is absent or is
`client_secret_basic` / `client_secret_post` — and is returned
exactly once.

400.description:
`invalid_request`. The messages include:
  * "unsupported grant_type: {value}"
  * "invalid JSON body"
  * "tenant_id is required when using the platform token"
  * "unsupported token_endpoint_auth_method: {value}"
  * "redirect_uris is required for the authorization_code grant"
  * "invalid initiate_login_uri: {why}"

When the client was created and a later step of the request failed, the body also carries `client_id`, and `client_secret` for a confidential client: the client exists.

404.description: `not_found` — "the management API is disabled".

409.description: `conflict` — "client already exists". Reachable only on a `client_id` collision, which the server generates itself.

500.description:
`server_error`: "could not secure client secret" when hashing the
generated secret fails, or "internal error" for any other
storage failure.

When the client was created and a later step of the request failed, the body also carries `client_id`, and `client_secret` for a confidential client: the client exists.

get.summary: List a tenant's clients, with its self-registration quota
get.description:
Everything in the tenant's client namespace, plus the quota that governs
self-registration. Inactive clients are included on purpose: "a disabled
client still holds its `client_id` in the tenant's namespace and still
counts against the registration quota, so a listing that hid it would say
'3 apps' while the quota said '5 used'".

`self_registered.used` is counted from the rows in this same response
rather than from a second query, "so the number and the list it describes
cannot disagree". `self_registered.source` says which level the
limit came from, because "a dashboard showing '100' with no hint it is the
deployment default invites an operator to PATCH the tenant to 100 and
believe they changed something".

NOT PAGINATED — `limit` is ignored and every row is returned. The
`used` derivation is only correct while that stays true.
get.x-auth:
auth.tenant_scope(q.tenant_id)                                            // :837
auth.require_any_scope_if_restricted(&[SCOPE_APPS_READ, SCOPE_APPS_WRITE]) // :841
"apps:write" satisfies this read (tests/management_api.rs).

parameters.name: tenant_id
parameters.description:
REQUIRED when authenticating with the platform bootstrap token —
omitting it is 400 `invalid_request`. With a tenant API key
it may be omitted (the key's own tenant is used) or supplied,
but a different tenant's id is 403 `forbidden`. A value
that is not a UUID is rejected with a 400
whose body is PLAIN TEXT, not the `{error, message}` shape.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description:
ACCEPTED AND IGNORED: an unknown query parameter is not an error here,
and this operation reads no `limit`. `limit` IS honoured on
`GET /api/v1/audit`. Sending it here changes nothing and the full result
set is returned; this listing is deliberately unpaged.

200.description: The tenant's clients and its self-registration quota.

400.description:
`invalid_request` — "tenant_id is required when using the platform
token". Separately, a non-UUID `tenant_id` produces a
plain-text 400 with no JSON body.

404.description: `not_found` — "the management API is disabled".

500.description: `server_error` — "internal error", when either the client list or the tenant's quota cannot be read.

delete.summary: Delete a SELF-REGISTERED client (the operator's release valve)
delete.description:
Deletes a client that arrived through RFC 7591 self-registration, and
nothing else. It exists because without it a registration quota is a
weapon rather than a defence: nothing else removes clients — no
background sweep expires them, and the only other DELETE is the RFC
7592 route that requires the client's own registration access token. An
attacker who fills a tenant to its cap and discards those tokens would
otherwise leave that tenant's registration endpoint dead permanently,
with direct database access as the only remedy.

It cannot touch an operator-provisioned client — one created by
`POST /api/v1/apps` or by `admin-cli seed-client`. Deleting a client
cascades to its tokens and consents, so that restriction is enforced by
the delete itself rather than by a check in front of it: the blast radius
of a mistyped `client_id` deserves more than an `if`.

There is no bulk form: recovering a tenant filled to 100 is a script.

parameters.name: client_id
parameters.description:
The client's `client_id` string — NOT a UUID. Nothing validates its
shape; an unmatched value is answered 404.

parameters.name: tenant_id
parameters.description: Required with the platform token (400 otherwise); must be the key's own tenant otherwise (403). Non-UUID values are a plain-text 400.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: ACCEPTED AND IGNORED. It has no meaning on a delete.

parameters.name: X-Proteles-Operator
parameters.description:
Asserted operator for the `app.deleted` audit row. Platform token
only; ignored (warn-logged) for a tenant key. Charset
`[A-Za-z0-9._\-@+:%]`, 1-256 bytes; anything else, or a repeated
header, is recorded as `(rejected)`.

204.description: Deleted; empty body. An `app.deleted` audit row is written first.

400.description: `invalid_request` — "tenant_id is required when using the platform token".

404.description:
`not_found` — "no self-registered client with that id". Two different
facts under one answer: no such client, and the client exists but was
operator-provisioned. "Indistinguishable on purpose … so this endpoint
cannot be used to enumerate which clients an operator created".
The same status with the message "the management API is disabled"
means the control plane is off.

500.description: `server_error` — "could not delete the client". A distinct message from the generic "internal error" other operations answer with.

patch.description:
The write path for a client an operator provisioned. Before this endpoint
only RFC 7592 could update a client, and RFC 7592
needs a registration access token that `POST /api/v1/apps` deliberately
does not issue — "handing it a self-management credential would mean
anyone who obtained that token could rewrite an app the operator
created". `DELETE` refuses those clients too, so there was no
delete-and-recreate escape either: moving a production callback domain
meant direct database access.

**Partial.** A field that is absent is left alone. There is no way to
clear one — an empty list is spelled `[]`, and no field is nullable.

**The settable set is exactly what `POST /api/v1/apps` sets.** Anything
creation hard-codes stays hard-coded: `require_pkce` is `true` there and
unreachable here, and `client_type` / `token_endpoint_auth_method` decide
how the client authenticates and are not a routine edit. A PATCH surface
wider than the POST one could reach configurations no creation call can
produce.

**Auth:** platform (naming a tenant), an unscoped tenant key, or a key
holding `apps:write`.

**Audit:** `app.updated`, naming the fields that changed and never their
values. `info`, except when `first_party` is among them — that flip stops
the consent screen appearing, so it is recorded at `warning`.

parameters.name: client_id
parameters.description: The client's `client_id`, as returned by `POST /api/v1/apps`.

200.description: The client as it now stands.

400.description: `invalid_request`: invalid JSON body, an unknown field, an empty `client_name` or `grant_types`, a grant type outside the supported set ("unsupported grant_type: {value}"), no fields at all, or an `authorization_code` grant left with no `redirect_uris`, or an `initiate_login_uri` that breaks its rule ("invalid initiate_login_uri: {why}") against the `redirect_uris` the app will have.

404.description: `not_found`: no client with that id **in this tenant**. Identical to the answer for a client that exists under another tenant, so this cannot enumerate them.

get.summary: Search the tenant's audit trail
get.description:
The durable security trail, newest first — ties in time broken by write
order, latest first — filtered and paged, as far back as the tenant's plan keeps it visible (3 days on FREE, 14 on TEAM, 60 on BUSINESS, read from the plan in force on every request). Rows are deleted a week after they leave that window. `event_type` is drawn from a
fixed vocabulary "so downstream tooling can rely on stable names";
`severity` is `info` or `warning`, where
warning "marks the security-suspicious ones … so an audit consumer can
filter for them".

`detail` is a free-form `k=v` string, never structured, and never
secrets — "hashes/ids only". When a platform caller
sent `X-Proteles-Operator`, the claim is appended to `detail` as
`asserted_operator=…` by the server; it is recorded *beside* the
credential in `by=`, never instead of it, and the key says `asserted_`
because nothing verified it. A tenant API key's
operator header is ignored with a warning log.

The stored row also carries an `id` which this endpoint does
**not** return, deliberately: that id is a sequence shared by every
tenant, so returning it would tell each tenant how many rows all the others
had written.

This paragraph used to end "so there is no cursor, and `limit` is the only
control" — in an operation that declares a `cursor` parameter and returns
`next_cursor`. Paging arrived; the sentence did not move. The cursor is a
keyset one and is **sealed**, an authenticated ciphertext over the position
and the tenant, precisely so that paging does not reintroduce the leak that
withholding `id` avoids.

x-auth.tenant-key: require_scope_if_restricted(SCOPE_AUDIT_READ) — management.rs. Only `audit:read`; unlike the webhook and app listings there is no write sibling that also satisfies it.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: Default 50, clamped to 1–500. Note the ceiling is 500 here and 200 on the two webhook listings.

parameters.name: event_type
parameters.description: Comma-separated event types, matched as OR. Empty or absent is no constraint — never "match nothing", which would make a cleared filter hide the whole trail.

parameters.name: severity
parameters.description: Comma-separated severities: `info`, `warning`, `critical`, each matched exactly — `warning` is warnings only, so a consumer who wants the critical rows too asks for both. Same empty-means-unfiltered rule as `event_type`.

parameters.name: actor_user_id
parameters.description: Only events about this user — the subject, the person the event concerns, not the one who acted. `mfa.admin_reset`, `password.reset_by_operator`, `sessions.revoked`, `user.deactivated` and `user.reactivated` are all recorded against the person affected, although somebody else caused them, which is what makes `GET /account/activity` a record of what happened *to* someone. Use `caused_by_user_id` for the other question: who did it.

parameters.name: caused_by_user_id
parameters.description: Only events this console member performed — "everything this administrator did". The other end of `actor_user_id`, and the two are not interchangeable: an administrator who deactivates an account appears here on that row, and the deactivated user appears in `actor_user_id`. Only a console member, a tenant's own admin acting in the dashboard; a platform operator appears as `asserted_operator` inside `detail_json`, and a management API key or `admin-cli` is named in `detail` because there is no user behind it.

parameters.name: client_id
parameters.description: Only events attributed to this OAuth client.

parameters.name: since
parameters.description: RFC 3339 instant, inclusive. A value that does not parse is refused rather than ignored — answering a time-range question with the whole trail, silently, is worse than refusing. It cannot reach past the tenant's plan window (3 days on FREE, 14 on TEAM, 60 on BUSINESS): an earlier `since` returns the window, and rows older than it are not returned at all.

parameters.name: until
parameters.description: RFC 3339 instant, exclusive, so `[midnight, next midnight)` counts each row once and adjacent day ranges cannot both contain the boundary row.

parameters.name: cursor
parameters.description: From a previous response's `next_cursor`. Keyset, not offset: the trail is appended to while it is read, so an offset shifts under the reader. A cursor this API did not issue is refused, because a client paging with a corrupted one would otherwise loop over page one forever. The value is sealed: it is an authenticated ciphertext over the position and the tenant, so it cannot be read, forged, or used by another tenant. That is not tidiness — the position includes the row's stored id, which is a sequence shared by every tenant, so a readable cursor told each tenant how many rows every other tenant had written. Treat it as opaque and hand it back unchanged.

200.description: Matching events, newest first, with a cursor for the next page.

get.summary: Download the filtered trail as NDJSON
get.description:
The same filters, the same row shape, as a file. One JSON object per line.

**Every response ends with a summary line**, and that is what makes it safe to save:

```
{"kind":"row","event_type":"login.success",…}
{"kind":"row","event_type":"login.failure",…}
{"kind":"summary","complete":true,"rows":2,"next_cursor":null}
```

A truncated export that looks complete is the failure this avoids. A response header would not survive `curl -o audit.ndjson`; a trailing line does — and a transfer that died mid-flight has no trailer at all, which is also detectable. Read `complete`; when it is false, request again with `cursor` set to `next_cursor`.

**Not CSV, deliberately.** CSV is what a customer opens, and it cannot carry `detail_json` without either flattening the structure away or quoting a JSON document inside a cell. The first is lossy about the only machine-readable half of the row; the second is a spreadsheet-shaped footgun.

**Paged rather than streamed**, at most 5000 rows per request. Streaming would need an async-stream dependency inside the authorization server's trust boundary to solve a problem paging already solves — and a long-lived response is what times out for exactly the tenant with a year of trail.

**Auth:** `audit:read`, the same scope as the list.

auth.tenant_scope(q.tenant_id)
auth.require_scope_if_restricted(audit:read)

parameters.name: until
parameters.description: RFC 3339 instant, exclusive, so `[midnight, next midnight)` counts each row once and adjacent day ranges cannot both contain the boundary row.

parameters.name: cursor
parameters.description: From a previous response's `next_cursor`. Keyset, not offset: the trail is appended to while it is read, so an offset shifts under the reader. A cursor this API did not issue is refused, because a client paging with a corrupted one would otherwise loop over page one forever. The value is sealed: it is an authenticated ciphertext over the position and the tenant, so it cannot be read, forged, or used by another tenant. That is not tidiness — the position includes the row's stored id, which is a sequence shared by every tenant, so a readable cursor told each tenant how many rows every other tenant had written. Treat it as opaque and hand it back unchanged.

200.description: NDJSON: zero or more `kind:"row"` lines, then exactly one `kind:"summary"`.

400.description: `invalid_request`: a malformed instant or a cursor this API did not issue.

post.summary: Create or replace a tenant's "sign in with X" connection
post.description:
Configures one social provider for one tenant. Upsert semantics: there is
no create-vs-update distinction and no 201 — a first configuration and a
rotation of an existing secret both answer 200.

The submitted `client_secret` is encrypted with the tenant's own data key
before storage, "so one tenant's leaked key can never expose another's
connection secrets", and is never echoed back by this
endpoint or by the listing.

Two cache effects, and they fail differently. This node's per-tenant OIDC
registry is dropped immediately so the change takes effect on the next
login. Other nodes are told via a cache-epoch bump — and if
that bump fails, the request still succeeds with 200 while logging an
error, because "a lost bump leaves them serving the previous client secret
with nothing to indicate it". A 200 therefore does not
guarantee every replica has the new secret.
post.x-auth:
auth.tenant_scope(req.tenant_id)                            // :1902
auth.require_scope_if_restricted(SCOPE_CONNECTIONS_WRITE)   // :1906  ("connections:write")

parameters.name: X-Proteles-Operator
parameters.description: Asserted operator for the `connection.updated` audit row. Platform token only; ignored for a tenant key. Charset `[A-Za-z0-9._\-@+:%]`, 1-256 bytes, else `(rejected)`.

200.description: Configured. The stored secret is not included.

400.description:
`invalid_request`, one of six messages:
  * "invalid JSON body" — malformed JSON, wrong content-type, OR any
    of the four required fields missing: `provider`, `client_id`,
    `client_secret` and `redirect_uri` are all required, and a body
    missing one is refused as a whole. A caller who omits one field is not told
    which.
  * "unsupported provider; expected one of google, github, linkedin,
    facebook"
  * "client_id, client_secret and redirect_uri are required" — the
    emptiness check
  * "redirect_uri must be this server's callback on a host of this
    tenant: {scheme}://{tenant host}/login/{provider}/callback" — see
    `redirect_uri` in the request schema
  * "redirect_uri must be written as {the same address}: it is sent to the
    provider exactly as stored" — the right callback, written another
    way (a leading space, a tab, a `.` segment, a capital in the host, a
    default port); the message names the spelling to send
  * "tenant_id is required when using the platform token"

404.description: `not_found` — "the management API is disabled".

500.description: `server_error` — "could not secure client secret" when tenant envelope encryption fails, or "internal error" when it cannot be stored, or "internal error" when the tenant's hosts could not be read to judge `redirect_uri` — the address is not blamed for an answer the store could not give.

get.summary: List the tenant's configured social connections
get.description:
Which providers are configured and whether each is enabled. "Secrets are
never returned; only whether each provider is configured and enabled"
— neither the secret nor its encrypted form appears.

Not paginated; `limit` is accepted and never read, so even a non-integer value is not refused.
get.x-auth:
auth.tenant_scope(q.tenant_id)                                                          // :1961
auth.require_any_scope_if_restricted(&[SCOPE_CONNECTIONS_READ, SCOPE_CONNECTIONS_WRITE]) // :1965
"connections:write" satisfies this read (tests/management_api.rs).

parameters.name: tenant_id
parameters.description: Required with the platform token (400 otherwise); must be the key's own tenant otherwise (403). Non-UUID values are a plain-text 400.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: ACCEPTED AND IGNORED — see `GET /api/v1/apps`. Nothing here reads `limit`, and an unknown query parameter is not an error.

200.description: The tenant's connections.

400.description: `invalid_request` — "tenant_id is required when using the platform token".

404.description: `not_found` — "the management API is disabled".

delete.summary: Remove a tenant's upstream login connection
delete.description:
The only way to remove one configured connection and keep the tenant,
and the answer to a question `POST /api/v1/connections` cannot answer.

That endpoint requires a non-empty `client_secret` and overwrites the
stored one, so an operator who had lost or rotated away the upstream
secret could only take a provider out of service by supplying a fabricated
one — destroying the real credential, leaving a permanent row whose
encrypted secret for a decommissioned provider lived at rest indefinitely,
and which a one-field POST could flip back on. Before this endpoint, removing
one took direct SQL. `DELETE /api/v1/tenants/{tenant_id}` also removes
a tenant's connections, along with everything else the tenant owns
except its audit trail.

**Removing, not disabling.** `enabled` already covers "off for now". This
covers "gone", and takes the encrypted upstream secret with it.

Invalidates this node's cached OIDC registry and bumps the tenant's cache
epoch, so other nodes stop offering the provider rather than serving it
until they restart.

**Auth:** platform (naming a tenant), an unscoped tenant key, or a key
holding `connections:write`.

**Audit:** `connection.deleted`, at **warning** — `connection.updated` is
info, but this one ends a sign-in route for every user who was using it.

parameters.name: provider
parameters.description: The provider key, e.g. `google`. A provider this tenant never configured is a 404.

parameters.name: tenant_id
parameters.description: Required when using the platform token, which will not guess a tenant.

404.description: `not_found`: no such connection **for this tenant**. Identical to the answer for one that belongs to another tenant, so this cannot enumerate them.

post.summary: Provision a new tenant
post.description:
Creates a tenant: the unit of isolation the whole server is built
around. A tenant owns its users, clients, keyring, branding, MFA policy
and audit trail, and every tenant-scoped read or write inside the server takes its id,
so a query cannot be issued without naming one.

The slug is a DNS label, not a display string. It is what
`<slug>.<base host>` resolves through, so it is stored lowercased —
accepting `ACME` verbatim minted a tenant whose own subdomain resolved
to nothing, and that is now a 404 on every request to it rather
than a fallback.

**Auth:** platform bootstrap token only. A tenant API key gets 403
`forbidden`.

**It creates nobody in the tenant.** A new tenant has no account and no owner, so nobody can open its console. `owner_email` records a contact address and nothing more. To give the tenant its owner, follow this with `POST /api/v1/tenants/{tenant_id}/owner-invitations`; the operator dashboard does both when its form is given an owner's address.

**Audited** as `tenant.created`, carrying the slug, how it was provisioned
and the owner address, against the tenant that was just created so the row
lives in that tenant's own trail.

This paragraph used to read "**Not audited.** … creating a tenant leaves no
audit row" — true when written, and
false from the moment the row was added, because the fact that a tenant
exists had been the one control-plane event with nothing recording it.
Documentation that understates a control is the safer direction to be
wrong in and still wrong: it is read by people deciding whether this
product can be audited.

requestBody.description:
`application/json` is required — any body that cannot be read
(missing/blank content-type, malformed body, wrong shape) is answered
with 400 `invalid_request` "invalid JSON body".

201.description:
Created. `status` is the default, `active`.
Note the body carries **no `display_name`** — no endpoint in this
group ever reads it back.

400.description: `invalid_request`. For the slug, the message names the specific rule that refused it — one of "slug must not be empty", "slug must be at most 63 characters; that one is N", "slug may contain only letters, digits and hyphens", "slug must not start or end with a hyphen", or "that slug is reserved". An `owner_email` that is given and is not a bare address: "owner_email must be an email address".

409.description: `conflict` — "a tenant with that slug already exists".

get.summary: Every tenant on the platform
get.description:
Backs the dashboard's tenant picker.

A per-tenant API key is **refused outright** rather than being narrowed
to its own tenant, "so this can never become a cross-tenant enumeration
path".

**Auth:** platform bootstrap token only.

**Unbounded.** No query parameters, no limit, no cursor: the response is
every tenant, oldest first, then by slug.

200.description: Every tenant.

get.summary: A tenant with its branding and second-factor policy
get.description:
The read model behind every tenant settings screen. It returns the
rollout window in three forms on purpose: `mfa_required_since` and
`mfa_grace_until` accompany `mfa_grace_days` "because '14' on its own
does not tell an operator whether their users have thirteen days left or
none".

**Auth:** the platform token unconditionally; a
tenant key for **this** tenant that declares no scopes at all; or a
tenant key holding `tenant:read` **or** `tenant:write` — the write scope
satisfies its read sibling, "a key trusted to change a thing is trusted
to see it".

Isolation is decided **before** scope here: a tenant key naming a
different tenant gets `forbidden`, not `insufficient_scope`. Note
the four domain operations below check these two in the opposite order.

**A read failure is reported as absence, not as an error.** `branding`
and the MFA enforcement settings both fall back to their defaults when
they cannot be read, so a database fault on either reads as
"nothing configured" rather than a 500.

200.description: The tenant.

404.description:
`not_found` — either "the management API is disabled" or "no such
tenant".

The second is the answer to **any** failure to read the tenant, a
database connection failure included: it is reported as a missing tenant.

patch.summary: Change a tenant's branding, second-factor policy, or client quota
patch.description:
The one write path for tenant-level settings. Every field is optional
and omitting one leaves it alone — `branding` included: it merges
sub-field by sub-field, and `null` is how you clear one (see the
request schema). It was a whole-object replace once, and callers written
against that behaviour are the reason this paragraph exists.

The policy and its window travel in one request deliberately. Sent
separately, "a request that turns the requirement on *and* sets a window
would spend the moment between the two writes requiring a factor with no
window at all — and anyone signing in during it would be forced to enrol
on the spot". The server therefore
writes the window first, then the policy.

On success it returns the **full tenant** by delegating to `getTenant`, so the 200 body is identical to
`GET /api/v1/tenants/{tenant_id}` — including its 404 if the tenant does
not exist.

**Auth:** platform, or an unscoped tenant key,
or a key holding `tenant:write`.
**Additionally**, if `max_self_registered_clients` or `max_members` is
present *at all* (including as `null`), the caller must be the platform
token:
"without this every customer could
raise its own ceiling and the quota would be advisory".

**Audit**, every row at warning: `mfa.policy_changed` when the policy is
set and `mfa.grace_changed` when the window is (emitted after both
writes so the recorded deadline is the one in force);
`passkey.attestation_changed` when `passkey_attestation` is set;
`mfa.self_recovery_changed` whenever `mfa_self_recovery_hours` is sent,
`null` included; and `tenant.mfa_email_factor_changed` when
`mfa_email_factor_enabled` is. And
`tenant.branding_changed` when `branding` changes anything — the one
row here at info when it touches only the logo or the colour, at warning
when it sets or clears `app_name`, carrying what was set and cleared. The
two quotas, `max_self_registered_clients` and `max_members`, are **not**
audited.

requestBody.description:
`application/json` required; a body that cannot be read is 400
`invalid_request` "invalid JSON body". An empty object `{}` is legal and is
a no-op that still returns 200 with the tenant.

200.description: The tenant as it now stands (the `getTenant` body).

400.description:
`invalid_request`, one of:
  * "invalid JSON body"
  * 'mfa_policy must be one of "optional", "required", "passkey"'
    (the list is built from the policies the server knows, so it grows
    with them rather than with somebody's memory)
  * "mfa_grace_days must be between 0 and 730"
  * 'passkey_attestation must be "none" or "required"'
  * "mfa_self_recovery_hours must be between 1 and 720 (null turns
    self-service recovery off); …"
  * "max_self_registered_clients must be zero or more (null restores
    the deployment default)"
  * "max_self_registered_clients must be at most 2147483647 (null
    restores the deployment default)"
  * "max_members must be at least 1 (null removes the limit); a tenant
    with no members cannot be administered"
  * "max_members must be at most 2147483647 (null removes the limit)"
  * "branding.app_name must be at most 100 characters"
  * "branding.app_name must not contain control characters (line
    breaks, tabs, NUL)"
  * "branding.logo_uri must be at most 2048 bytes"
  * "branding.logo_uri must be an absolute https URL"

Every field is validated, and the platform gate applied, before
anything is written, so a 400 or 403 changes nothing — branding
included (it was once written ahead of the checks).

404.description: `not_found` — management API disabled, or "no such tenant" from the trailing `getTenant`.

409.description: `passkey_attestation: "required"` with no attestation CA registered. That state fails every registration, so it is refused rather than created. It is checked after the quotas and `mfa_grace_days` are written, so a 409 leaves those, and `branding`, already changed.

delete.summary: Delete a tenant and everything belonging to it
delete.description:
**Irreversible, and complete by construction rather than by a list.** Everything the tenant owns except its audit trail — its users, its apps and everything that belongs to either — is linked to the tenant so that deleting the tenant deletes it, in one step, with no list of things to remove for a maintainer to forget. A check on every change fails if any new kind of tenant-owned data is not linked that way.

**Four gates, checked in this order, each for a specific way this goes wrong.** The body is read between the first and the second: a missing or malformed body, one without `confirm_slug`, or one with any other field, is 400 "invalid JSON body" before anything else is looked at. A tenant that does not exist is 404 between the second and the third.
  * *Platform scope only.* A tenant's own key cannot delete its tenant (403). The trade: a customer cannot self-serve deletion, and a leaked tenant key cannot destroy the account it was issued for.
  * *Never the default tenant.* Naming it is 403 whatever its status and whatever `confirm_slug` says, once the body has been read. It holds the deployment's own signing keys, operator console and audit trail; deleting it is not a destructive operation somebody might mean, and no confirmation string should be able to express it.
  * *`confirm_slug` must match* (400). The realistic way to delete the wrong tenant is a stale or mistyped **id**, which is a uuid nobody reads. Naming the tenant in a form a human can check is what catches that.
  * *Suspended first.* A live tenant is refused with 409. Suspension already takes the tenant offline, so deletion becomes the second step of something already noticed.

**What is not deleted.** The tenant's audit trail remains: one hash chain covers every tenant, so removing one tenant's entries would break the sealed ranges for all of them. The mapping that would let audit entries name people by a random id is deleted with the tenant, but nothing uses it yet, so **retained audit entries may still contain identifiers** written into `detail`, which is sealed and permanent. The response says so in `audit_rows_may_contain_identifiers`; anyone answering a right-to-erasure request needs that fact rather than an assurance.

200.description: The tenant is gone. The body reports what went, counted before the delete, and states plainly that the audit rows stayed.

400.description: `invalid_request` — "invalid JSON body", or "confirm_slug does not match this tenant's slug".

404.description: `not_found` — no such tenant. Checked before `confirm_slug`, so a wrong id is not answered with a question about a tenant that does not exist.

409.description: `conflict` — "suspend this tenant before deleting it".

put.summary: Switch a tenant off, or back on
put.description:
Platform token only. A tenant key that could suspend its own tenant would be a
self-destruct button; one that could suspend another's would be worse.

Suspension is the abuse response for self-service signup, and it is why the write
path exists at all: host resolution already refuses any tenant that is not
active, so a non-active tenant 404s everywhere — nothing could put one in that state.
Suspending takes every one of that tenant's users offline: their hostname stops
resolving and every request to it 404s.

`deleted` is deliberately not accepted, though the stored status can hold
it. Removing a tenant means removing its users' data and its signing
keys; a status that merely reads as deleted while every row stays in place is the
kind of thing an operator would rely on and be wrong about.

Audited as `tenant.status_changed` at **warning**, in both directions, carrying the
status it actually replaced — re-suspending an already-suspended tenant is not the
event the first suspension was, and only one of them took anybody offline.

200.description: The new status, and the one it replaced.

400.description: `status` was neither "active" nor "suspended", or the body was not JSON.

404.description: No such tenant.

post.summary: Invite a workspace's owner by email
post.description:
Mails an owner invitation for a workspace, on the platform's authority. For a workspace nobody can administer: one made with `POST /api/v1/tenants`, which creates no account in it, or one whose owners have left. On a deployment that cannot send mail, `admin-cli seed-user` and then `admin-cli grant-owner` on the server remain the way to give a workspace its owner.

**The console's owner invitation, sent by the platform.** The same table, link, mail and accept page as the console's: only the token's SHA-256 is stored, it is spent by a single atomic write, so it works once, it expires in 72 hours, it is mailed to the address it names, and it is never returned to the caller — whoever could read the link could accept it themselves, under somebody else's address, as the workspace's owner. Accepting creates the account and grants `owner`. An address that already has an account in the workspace becomes that account's owner only when whoever opens the link enters that account's own password, and not at all when that account never confirmed the address. The grant is held to the workspace's seat cap like any other.

**Marked as the platform's.** Acceptance refuses a role invitation whose sender is no longer an owner of the workspace. Nobody in the workspace sent this one, so it carries a mark of its own, written by this operation and by nothing else, and acceptance skips that one check for it. A role invitation that names no sender because its sender's account was deleted is not marked, and is still refused.

**Through the deployment's relay only.** The mail goes through the deployment's own relay (`SMTP_HOST`), never through one the workspace configured with `PUT /api/v1/mail`. A workspace's relay is set with a workspace key holding `mail:write`, and in a workspace with no owner whoever holds such a key could otherwise point it at a server of their own and open the owner's link first.

**No token without a way to deliver it.** A deployment with no relay of its own is refused with 409 `mail_not_configured`, whatever relay the workspace has, and no invitation is created. A relay that fails the send is reported as `delivered: false`: the invitation exists by then, and can be sent again.

**Not held to the self-service invitation allowance.** The platform vouches by sending, so a workspace self-service sign-up made can be given an owner even when none of its owners has confirmed an address. The send is recorded as the console's is, `tenant_invitation.sent`, so it counts among that workspace's invitations for the day.

**Refused for a suspended workspace** (409 `conflict`): acceptance would refuse an invitation into one.

**What it replaces.** A second invitation to the same address, from here or from the console, leaves only the newest link working. And the platform keeps one live owner invitation per workspace: sending to another address withdraws the platform's earlier live one there — a mistyped address, say — and names it in `replaced`. While this invitation is live, a workspace key's end-user invitation to the same address (`POST /api/v1/users/invite`) is refused with 409 rather than replacing it; an owner's invitation from the console replaces it, as it replaces any other.

**Withdrawn with `DELETE`** on this path, which takes the same body.

**Auth:** platform token only. A tenant key is refused with 403, whatever its scopes.

**Audit:** `tenant_invitation.sent` (warning), with `invited_by: "platform-token"` where the console's names a member; `tenant_invitation.revoked` with `revoked_by: "platform-token"` and `replaced_by` for each invitation in `replaced`; on acceptance, `tenant_member.granted` with `granted_by: "platform-token"`, naming the account that received the role.

202.description: Accepted. Nothing is granted until somebody opens the link, and it may never be opened. `delivered` says whether the mail went out; the invitation is live either way.

400.description: `invalid_request` — the body was not JSON, named a field other than `email`, or `email` is not a bare address: more than 254 bytes, no `@`, whitespace or a control character in it, or anything but an addr-spec at a host name — a display name, angle brackets, a comment, a list, a quoted local part, or a domain with no dot, an IP address or another bracketed literal.

404.description: `not_found` — no such tenant, or the Management API is disabled on this deployment.

409.description: Nothing was sent and no invitation was created. `conflict` — the workspace is suspended. `mail_not_configured` — the deployment has no mail relay of its own (`SMTP_HOST`), and an owner invitation goes through nothing else, whatever relay the workspace has. Configure the deployment's relay and send it again, or give the workspace its owner with `admin-cli`.

500.description: `server_error` — this deployment declares no tenant base host, so no invitation link can be built; or the invitation could not be stored.

delete.description:
Withdraws the live owner invitation the platform sent an address (`POST` on this path), so its link stops working. For the invitation that went to the wrong address: nobody in a workspace without an owner can withdraw one from the console, which needs an owner.

Only what the platform sent. An invitation an owner sent from the console, or a workspace key's end-user invitation, to the same address is left alone and answers `withdrawn: false`, as does an address with no live invitation — accepted, expired, or never sent. That is an answer, not an error. Allowed for a suspended workspace.

Sending to the corrected address withdraws the mistyped one too, since the platform keeps one live owner invitation per workspace; this is for taking one back without sending another.

The address is looked up, not held to the address rule `POST` applies: trimmed, not blank, free of control characters, and matched case-insensitively against what was sent. So an invitation sent before the rule was tightened — one with a quoted local part, which `POST` once took — can still be withdrawn.

**Auth:** platform token only. A tenant key is refused with 403, whatever its scopes.

**Audit:** `tenant_invitation.revoked`, with `revoked_by: "platform-token"`, when something was withdrawn.

200.description: Whether a live invitation from the platform was withdrawn.

400.description: `invalid_request` — the body was not JSON, named a field other than `email`, or `email` is blank once trimmed ("email must not be empty") or holds a control character ("email must not contain a control character"). It is not held to the address rule `POST` applies: it is only looked up.

404.description: `not_found` — no such tenant, or the Management API is disabled on this deployment.

500.description: `server_error` — the invitation could not be withdrawn.

post.summary: Rotate the tenant's data encryption key
post.description:
Mints **new DEK material**. Everything sealed from now on uses it.

Not to be confused with two neighbours that also say 'key':
`/keys/rotate` rotates the tenant's *signing* key, and `admin-cli
rewrap-data-keys` re-wraps the *same* DEK under a new KEK. Only this one
changes the key bytes that seal tenant secrets, which is what 'rotate the
key' means after a suspected disclosure.

**Existing secrets are not re-encrypted and remain readable.** Every
ciphertext carries the DEK version that sealed it, so v1 values keep
decrypting under v1 while new values use v2. Moving old ciphertext onto the
new key rewrites customer data and is deliberately a separate operation.

Audited as `data_key.rotated` at warning.

200.description: The new version, and the one it replaced.

409.description: `rotation_too_soon` — a workspace's own API key already rotated this key in the last hour. A workspace key may rotate it once an hour; the platform credential is not limited. Nothing changes.

503.description: `unavailable` — the audit trail could not be read to check when the data key was last rotated. Nothing changes; try again.

500.description: The rotation failed; nothing was changed.

post.summary: Claim a custom hostname for a tenant
post.description:
Step one of two. A claim "records an intent and resolves nothing"; the
row only becomes live once `POST .../verify` reads a TXT record that
only the domain's owner could have published. Until then host
resolution will not match it, so an unverified claim serves no traffic.

The response carries everything needed to finish: the record type, the
exact name to publish at, and the token.

**Auth — strict scope, and the only strict one under
`/api/v1/tenants/{tenant_id}`:** `domains:write`. An **unscoped tenant
key is refused**. The reason is what it grants: "the ability to make a
hostname serve this tenant's login page, which is a phishing page with a
real password field if it is pointed somewhere it should not be". An
unscoped key passes every held-to-what-you-declare check, so under a held
rule every unscoped key would have that. `TenantApiKeyScope` lists the
other strict operations. There is **no** `domains:read` — the same scope gates
the list.

**Check order is inverted relative to `getTenant`.** Scope is tested
first, tenant isolation second. So a tenant key
without `domains:write` that names a foreign tenant sees
`insufficient_scope`, where `GET /api/v1/tenants/{id}` would have said
`forbidden`. Same status, different code.

**Audit:** `tenant_domain.claimed`.

201.description:
Claimed, unverified. `verified` is `false` and `verified_at` is
`null`; publish `challenge.value` as a TXT record at
`challenge.name`, then call the verify endpoint.

400.description:
`invalid_request` — "invalid JSON body", or "domain must be a bare
hostname with at least one dot — no scheme, port, path, or wildcard".
See the request schema for the exact rules.

409.description:
`conflict`, one of two:

* "that hostname is one this deployment already routes; it would
  never reach the custom-domain table": a base host itself, or
  exactly one label under a base host, which host resolution reads as
  a tenant slug. The check asks host resolution's own rule rather than
  re-deriving it, because "this check used to mirror the equality case
  and miss the slug case, which is precisely the drift that produces
  an inert row that looks configured".
* "that domain is already claimed by this workspace" — this
  tenant's own earlier claim, and only that. Another tenant's claim,
  verified or not, does not stop this one: an unverified claim never
  held a name, and a verified one is contested by proving the
  name (`.../verify`). So the answer says nothing about
  another customer.

get.summary: A tenant's domain claims, verified or not
get.description:
Returns every claim with its challenge token, so an operator can see
what is still outstanding and what to publish. The token is not a secret
in the usual sense — it ends up in public DNS — "but it is only ever
shown to the caller who holds a management key for the tenant that
claimed the domain, because being *told* the token is what lets you
finish somebody's claim".

**Auth:** `domains:write` — the write scope, because there is
no `domains:read` scope.
An unscoped tenant key cannot read this list.

**Unbounded.** No query parameters, no limit; oldest first.

200.description: The tenant's claims.

delete.description:
Drops the row, verified or not. If it was verified the hostname stops
serving that tenant **immediately** — host resolution has nothing left to
match, which is why the audit row
records what it cost.

The claim is read before the delete "so the audit row can say whether a
live hostname just went dark — the difference between releasing a typo
and causing an outage".

**Auth:** `domains:write` (strict), then tenant isolation.

**Audit:** `tenant_domain.removed`, severity warning, detail
`domain=<d> was_verified=<bool>`.

404.description:
`not_found` — management API disabled, or "no such domain claim",
whether the claim is missing when it is first read or when it is
deleted. Another tenant's claim lands here too: the read and the
delete are both keyed on the tenant and the domain.

post.summary: Prove a domain claim by DNS
post.description:
Step two. Reads TXT records at `_proteles-challenge.<domain>` and
compares them, in constant time, against the token issued with the claim. A match stamps
`verified_at`, and only then does host resolution match the hostname.

DNS rather than an HTTP challenge, because a
custom login domain points at *this* server, so an HTTP challenge "would
be fetched from us, served by us, and would prove only that we can talk
to ourselves. DNS is the one channel the domain's owner controls and this
server does not".

**Idempotent on success.** An already-verified domain verifies again
without moving `verified_at` — the first proof's time is kept —
"so a client that retries does not make a stale proof look fresh".

**Bounded:** one attempt may spend at most 5 seconds
in DNS, "because this runs inside a management API request… without a
ceiling it becomes the request's latency".

**Auth:** `domains:write` (strict), then tenant isolation.

**Audit:** `tenant_domain.verified` on success;
`tenant_domain.verification_failed` with
`reason=no_record` or `reason=mismatch` on a 400. A 503 is **not** audited — it is not
a failed proof.

requestBody.description: None. A body is not read; send it empty.

200.description:
Proved. Note this is a *different, smaller* shape than the claim
object — `{domain, verified}` only, no `created_at`, no
`verified_at`, no `challenge`.

400.description:
`verification_failed` — the owner's to fix. The message is
`"<reason>. Publish a TXT record at _proteles-challenge.<domain>
with the value from this claim."` where `<reason>` is either "no
challenge record found" or "the challenge record does
not match the token we issued".

Also 400 for a `tenant_id` path segment that is not a UUID — refused
before the operation runs, plain text, no `error` field.

404.description:
`not_found` — management API disabled, or "no such domain claim".
The lookup is tenant-scoped "so a key cannot read another tenant's
challenge token — being told the token is what would let you finish
their claim". Also returned if the claim is
deleted between the read and the write, rather than a 500.

409.description:
`conflict`, one of three:

* "this claim has no challenge token; remove it and claim
the domain again". A claim from before verification existed, or one
whose token was cleared, has no token to compare against. Inventing a token
here "would verify a claim nobody had been asked to prove".
* "that domain is verified by another workspace, and its record still
proves it". **A contest**: this proof succeeded, another
tenant holds the name verified, and the holder's own record was read again
and still proves theirs. Had it not (no record, or one that does not match),
the name would have moved here — 200 — and the holder been told in its
trail (`tenant_domain.lost`). DNS that cannot answer the re-read is a 503 and
moves nothing. The reply never names the holder.
* "that domain changed hands while this proof was checked; verify again".

503.description:
`dns_unavailable` — "could not read DNS for that domain; this is not
a failed proof — try again".
Timeout, network failure or broken resolver config. Kept distinct
from 400 because "telling a tenant 'your DNS is wrong' because our
resolver timed out sends them to edit a zone that was already
correct". Retryable; not audited.

post.summary: Mint a management API key for a tenant
post.description:
Mints an `mk_…` bearer that authenticates management calls for exactly
one tenant. The raw key is returned **once** and never stored — only its
SHA-256.

**`scopes` is required and must name at least one scope**. A key with no scopes passes every held-to-what-you-declare
check, so it was the broadest mint there is, and no route mints one any
more; keys minted before keep working. The request also refuses unknown
fields, and a malformed body rather than defaulting it, so a misspelt
`scopes` is named as what it is — "every way of failing to say 'scopes' has to be an error".

**Auth:** platform bootstrap token only. The platform gate deliberately runs
*before* the tenant-existence lookup, "or the refusal leaks which tenants
exist".

**Audit:** `apikey.created`, with the key's id and name.

The 201 carries the key's `id`, which `DELETE .../keys/{key_id}` and
`POST .../keys/{key_id}/rotate` take, and which a SAML service provider
registration's audit rows written with the key record as `api_key_id`.

201.description: The raw key, shown for the only time.

400.description:
`invalid_request`, one of:
  * "invalid JSON body" — malformed, wrong types, **or any unknown
    field**. `{"scopez": [...]}` is a 400, not a silently unscoped key.
  * "unknown scope '<x>'; known scopes: <every mintable scope,
    comma-separated, in the order of the `TenantApiKeyScope` enum>"
  * "name at least one scope: a key with no scopes would have every
    permission, and none is minted; known scopes: <the same list>" —
    `scopes` omitted or `[]`. Nothing is written.

404.description: `not_found` — management API disabled, or "no such tenant".

get.summary: A tenant's API keys, metadata only
get.description:
Never returns the raw key or its hash. This exists because the list is
how an operator finds the id to revoke: without it, answering "which key
is that?" took direct database access, which is most of what made
revocation unreachable in the first place.

**Auth:** platform bootstrap token only.

**No tenant-existence check.** Unlike `POST` on the same path,
this goes straight to the list, so an unknown or already-deleted `tenant_id`
answers `200 {"keys": []}` rather than 404.

**Unbounded.** No query parameters, no limit; every key the tenant has
ever held, revoked ones included, newest first.

200.description: The tenant's keys.

parameters.name: key_id
parameters.description:
The key's `id`, as the mint response and `GET .../keys` return it —
**not** the raw `mk_…` value. A non-UUID segment
is rejected before the operation runs.

delete.description:
**Idempotent by intent.** Revoking an already-revoked key is 200, not
404, and the original revocation time stands: "whoever calls this is
containing a leak, and an error on the second attempt reads as 'the key
is still live' at the one moment that sentence must be reliable".

The key's name is read *before* the revocation so the audit row can name
it; if the read fails the name is recorded as `"unknown"`.

**Auth:** platform bootstrap token only, "matching who may mint. A tenant key
revoking its siblings would be a faster incident response and also a way
for one stolen key to switch off a tenant's automation".

**Audit:** `apikey.revoked`, severity warning, carrying the key id, its
name and the credential class that revoked it.

200.description: Revoked, or already was.

404.description:
`not_found` — management API disabled, or "no such API key for this
tenant". A key id belonging to a
*different* tenant lands here too: the lookup is scoped to the tenant,
so this is 404 rather than a cross-tenant revocation.

get.summary: Look one user up by exact username, with their second-factor status
get.description:
The first step of the operator support flow: "before disarming an
account, an operator should be able to confirm they have the right person
and see what they are about to remove".

Deliberately a lookup by EXACT username and not a listing, "so this is not
a bulk export of the tenant's user base". No prefix search, no
pagination, no enumeration.

It is also the only way to obtain the `user_id` that the two action
endpoints below take in their path.
get.x-auth:
auth.tenant_scope(q.tenant_id)                                  // :904
auth.require_any_scope_if_restricted(
    &[SCOPE_USERS_READ, SCOPE_RESET_MFA, SCOPE_REVOKE_SESSIONS]) // :911
The two ACTION scopes are accepted here as well as "users:read":
"resetting or revoking requires the user id, and this lookup is the only
way to get one — a key granted the action but not the lookup could never
use what it was given" (:908-910). Note the asymmetry with the actions
themselves, which use the strict `require_scope`: an UNSCOPED tenant key
passes this guard (held-to-what-you-declare) but is refused by both
actions.

parameters.name: username
parameters.description:
Exact match, no wildcards. REQUIRED — omitting it is rejected with a
400 whose body is PLAIN TEXT, not the `{error, message}` shape.
Authentication is checked first, so an unauthenticated caller gets 401,
not that 400.

parameters.name: tenant_id
parameters.description: Required with the platform token (400 otherwise); must be the key's own tenant otherwise (403).

200.description: The user and their current second-factor inventory.

400.description:
`invalid_request` — "tenant_id is required when using the platform
token". Separately, an absent `username` or a non-UUID
`tenant_id` produces a plain-text 400 with no JSON body.

404.description:
`not_found` — "no such user in this tenant". Covers both a
genuinely absent user and one belonging to another tenant: the lookup
is scoped by tenant rather than global-then-compared.
WORTH KNOWING: a DATABASE FAILURE during the lookup also surfaces as
404 rather than 500.
The same status with "the management API is disabled" means the
control plane is off.

get.x-no-500:
This operation has no 500 path. The user lookup collapses to 404 (above)
and the three MFA reads swallow their errors —
`passkeys.count(…).unwrap_or(0)` (:918) and `remaining_recovery_codes`
(mfa.rs) — so a failing datastore reports "0 passkeys, 0 recovery
codes" rather than an error.

post.summary: Create a password user in a tenant
post.description:
The supported way for a tenant provisioned through the dashboard or this
API to get its first username/password user. Before this endpoint the
options were `admin-cli seed-user --tenant <slug>`, which needs a shell on
the host, or configuring a social connection and having the first user
arrive through a federated sign-in.

**Create, not upsert.** A username already taken in this tenant is a 409;
it does not reset that user's password. `admin-cli seed-user` *does* upsert,
which is a reasonable convenience for somebody who already has the box, and
the wrong default over the network.

**Password floor:** 12 characters, the same as the self-service change at
`/account/password`. A rule that applied only to the form the user can see
would be a rule about forms rather than about passwords.

**Auth:** platform (naming a tenant), an unscoped tenant key, or a key
holding `users:write` — a new scope, distinct from
`users:read`, because reading a user and minting one that can sign in are
different authorities.

**Audit:** `user.created` (info). The record carries the new id and not the
username, which is user-supplied text on a trail that leaves the machine.

**Address trust:** `email_verified` defaults to `true`, which preserves the behaviour every tenant has today — social sign-in may link to an operator-created account. This field makes that trust explicit rather than incidental; send `false` if you are not in a position to vouch.

201.description: Created. The password is never echoed back.

400.description: `invalid_request`: invalid JSON body, an unknown field, an empty username, an `email` that is not a bare address ("email must be an email address"; see the request schema), or a password under 12 characters.

409.description: `conflict`: this tenant already has a user with that username; or the username is another account's email address, or the email address another account's username, either of which would make one name sign in to two accounts.

post.summary: Clear a user's second factors (the lost-phone response)
post.description:
"The way back in for someone who has lost both their authenticator and
their recovery codes. It is a backdoor by design, so it is: gated behind
an explicit scope, strictly tenant-scoped, audited at warning severity
with a required reason, and limited to *second* factors — it never touches
the primary credential, so it can weaken an account but never strand its
owner".

What it does, in order: reads whether a confirmed TOTP
enrolment and a pending one exist, **revokes every session first**, then
disables TOTP, then deletes every passkey. Revocation comes first and
is part of the reset itself, so that "reset without revoking" is not
possible — without it "the cookie that survived the reset could enrol a
brand new factor in one POST, with nothing to present, and that factor
outlived everything the operator had just cleared".

Under a `required` tenant MFA policy the user meets forced enrolment at
their next sign-in, which is the intended landing.

Side effects beyond the response: an `mfa.admin_reset` audit row at
`warning` severity carrying `totp=… passkeys=… pending=… reason=…`,
and a best-effort `mfa.admin_reset` webhook fired AFTER the
audit row because "the reset has already happened and must stand whether
or not anyone can be told about it". A webhook failure does
not affect the response.
post.x-auth:
auth.tenant_scope(req.tenant_id)              // :958
auth.require_scope(SCOPE_RESET_MFA)           // :962  ("users:reset_mfa")
STRICT, not held-to-what-you-declare: an UNSCOPED tenant key is REFUSED.
"Keys created before this endpoint existed were never granted the power to
disarm an account, and silently handing it to them would be a privilege
escalation introduced by a deploy" (:68-74). Pinned by
tests/mfa_admin_reset.rs.
post.x-rate-limit:
Its own tight bucket, "management_user_action", matched AHEAD of the
general `/api/v1/` arm: RATE_LIMIT_USER_ACTION_PER_MIN, default 10 per
minute (rate_limit/mod.rs, config.rs). "Without it, a key that
has legitimately been granted `users:reset_mfa` can disarm an entire
tenant account by account as fast as the network allows"
(rate_limit/mod.rs).

parameters.name: user_id
parameters.description:
A non-UUID is a plain-text 400. Authentication is checked first, so a
bad credential beats a bad UUID — 401 wins.

parameters.name: X-Proteles-Operator
parameters.description:
Asserted operator, recorded on the `mfa.admin_reset` audit row beside
the credential — "recorded alongside this, never in place of it, and
under a key that says it was asserted". Platform token
only; a tenant key's header is ignored and warn-logged.
Charset `[A-Za-z0-9._\-@+:%]`, 1-256 bytes; anything else, or a
repeated header, is recorded as `(rejected)`.

requestBody.description:
FORMALLY OPTIONAL, EFFECTIVELY REQUIRED. An absent body — no bytes at all —
is a request with no reason, and is answered "a reason is required". A body
that is present and cannot be read — malformed JSON, a wrong type, a content
type other than JSON, or an unknown key — is a 400 "invalid JSON body" and
resets nothing. It used to be read as absent too, and told a caller who had
sent a reason that one was required.

200.description:
Reset performed, possibly as a no-op. A user with no factors at all is
still a 200, with `totp_removed: false`, `passkeys_removed: 0` and the
"nothing changed" note.

400.description:
`invalid_request`:
  * "invalid JSON body" — a body that is present and cannot be read,
    see requestBody above; checked first
  * "a reason is required and is recorded in the audit log"
  * "tenant_id is required when using the platform token",
    checked BEFORE the reason

404.description:
`not_found` — "no such user in this tenant". The lookup is
tenant-scoped, so a foreign user id NOT accompanied by an explicit
foreign `tenant_id` reaches here rather than 403. As with the lookup, a
database failure also surfaces as 404. The same status with "the management API is disabled" means the
control plane is off.

500.description: `server_error` — "could not reset second factors", when the reset itself fails. Nothing has been audited or notified at that point.

post.summary: End every session and refresh token a user holds (the compromise response)
post.description:
Distinct from the MFA reset, which also revokes: this one leaves the
account's factors alone. That is the difference between "someone has their
session" and "they have lost their phone", and conflating them makes the
compromise response destroy credentials the user still holds and will need
to get back in.

What is actually killed: "sessions, the two half-login cookies, refresh
tokens, authorization codes and device codes — anything issued at or
before the returned instant is refused from the next request onward, on
every replica, with no cache to go stale". Access tokens already minted
are refused at introspection and userinfo too; only an API that verifies
the JWT without asking this server accepts one until it expires.
The response says so in `note` rather than letting "revoked" imply more
than it does.

Side effect: a `sessions.revoked` audit row at `warning` severity carrying
the reason and the acting credential. No webhook is fired — unlike the MFA
reset.
post.x-auth:
auth.tenant_scope(req.tenant_id)                  // :1056
auth.require_scope(SCOPE_REVOKE_SESSIONS)         // :1060  ("users:revoke_sessions")
STRICT: an unscoped tenant key is refused. Deliberately a SEPARATE scope
from "users:reset_mfa" and not implied by it — "an operator who can help
with a lost phone should not thereby be able to sign an executive out of
every device mid-quarter-end. Granting both to the same key is a decision,
not a default" (:82-88). Pinned by tests/mfa_admin_reset.rs.
post.x-rate-limit:
Shares the "management_user_action" bucket with the MFA reset:
RATE_LIMIT_USER_ACTION_PER_MIN, default 10/min (rate_limit/mod.rs,
config.rs). A shared budget is deliberate — "these guess no secret, so
spending one budget buys no progress against the other"
(rate_limit/mod.rs).

parameters.name: user_id
parameters.description: A non-UUID is a plain-text 400, and authentication is checked first, so a bad credential yields 401 instead.

parameters.name: X-Proteles-Operator
parameters.description: Asserted operator for the `sessions.revoked` audit row. Platform token only; ignored for a tenant key. Charset `[A-Za-z0-9._\-@+:%]`, 1-256 bytes, else `(rejected)`.

requestBody.description:
The same body handling as the MFA reset: an absent body is a request with no
reason, and a body that is present and cannot be read is a 400 "invalid JSON
body" that revokes nothing.

200.description: Every credential issued at or before `sessions_revoked_at` is now dead.

400.description:
`invalid_request` — "invalid JSON body" for a body that cannot be read,
checked first; "a reason is required and is recorded in the audit
log" (a whitespace-only reason counts as absent) — or "tenant_id is required when
using the platform token", which is checked before the reason.

404.description: `not_found` — "no such user in this tenant", including on a database failure during the lookup. Also "the management API is disabled".

500.description: `server_error` — "could not revoke sessions". Nothing has been audited at that point.

post.summary: Turn an account off and end its sessions
post.description:
Sets `is_active = false`, then revokes the account's sessions, in that order.

Both are needed: `is_active` is checked when a credential is *presented*, so a user who is
already signed in keeps working until their sessions are revoked too. Deactivating first
means the window between the two denies new sign-ins rather than allowing them.

Emits two audit rows: `user.deactivated` and `sessions.revoked`, both `warning`. Separate
rows because `sessions.revoked` is what an operator greps for when asking why a session
died — folding it into the deactivation detail would make that unanswerable here.

auth.require_scope(SCOPE_USERS_WRITE)   // STRICT, unlike createUser

  * "a reason is required — it is what the audit trail records"; a

post.summary: Turn an account back on
post.description:
Sets `is_active = true`. Does not restore sessions — revocation is not reversible, so the
user signs in again.

Emits `user.reactivated` at `warning`: handing access back is not more routine than taking
it away.
