get.summary: Events this tenant was never told about
get.description:
The queue of admitted losses. "a row here is not waiting for anything,
it is waiting for someone". Newest death
first.

Three numbers come back beside the page, and the scoping of each is
deliberate:

* `outstanding` is **tenant-wide and unfiltered** — not narrowed by
  `webhook_id`, not truncated by `limit`. "This is the number an alarm
  watches, and an alarm that goes quiet because someone applied a filter
  or because the list was truncated at fifty is worse than no alarm".
* `outstanding_by_endpoint` counts per endpoint, in the database rather
  than from the page, and covers **only endpoints that still exist**;
  letters orphaned by a deletion are inside `outstanding` with nothing
  to attribute them to.
* `retention_days` is the deployment's `DEAD_LETTER_RETENTION_DAYS`
  (default 90, floored at 0). It is "the configured policy, not a promise
  about a particular deployment's sweeper" — housekeeping may run from
  an external cron the server cannot see. `0` means acknowledged letters
  are kept indefinitely.

The lost `body` **is** included here, unlike in the delivery listing,
"because reconstructing it by hand from the event type and a timestamp
is exactly the work an operator should not have to do".

parameters.name: webhook_id
parameters.description: Narrows the `dead_letters` page only. `outstanding` ignores it by design.

parameters.name: include_acknowledged
parameters.description: Default `false`. "Off by default: the useful question is what is still unanswered, not what has ever failed, and a list that never shrinks is a list nobody reads".

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: Default 50, clamped to 1–200.

200.description: The counts, the policy, and a page of letters.

500.description: `server_error`. Three separate queries back this response — the page, the tenant-wide count, the per-endpoint breakdown — and a failure in any one of them fails the whole request.

post.summary: Mark dead letters as dealt with
post.description:
"Acknowledging is not a fix; it is a decision that these events will
never be delivered and that someone knows. That is why it is recorded,
and why it is separate from replaying: pressing replay says 'try
again', this says 'we are done trying'".

Acknowledged letters drop out of the default dead-letter view and out of
`outstanding`, and become eligible for the retention sweep.

Omission semantics — and this is the operation where absent and empty
are most consequential:

* `ids` omitted **or** `[]` means **every outstanding letter matching
  `webhook_id`**.
  Absent and empty are the same, and both mean "all".
* `webhook_id` omitted means every endpoint, so `{}` acknowledges the
  tenant's entire outstanding queue.
* The **whole body may be absent** — no bytes at all — and the call
  takes those defaults. A body that is **present and cannot be read** —
  malformed JSON, a wrong type, a content type other than JSON, or an
  unknown key — is a 400 and acknowledges nothing. It used to be read as
  absent, so a typo in `ids` acknowledged the whole queue.

Audited as `webhook.dead_letters_acknowledged` only when at least one
letter was acknowledged.

200.description: How many letters were acknowledged.

400.description:
`invalid_request`, one of:
* "invalid JSON body" — a body that is present and cannot be read,
  checked first, and nothing is acknowledged;
* "tenant_id is required when using the platform token" — only a
  tenant API key may leave it out, because that key already is one.

post.summary: Delete the named dead letters
post.description:
The only call in the subsystem that destroys the record of something
going wrong. It was single-only for a while;
the bulk form exists because "after a decommissioned endpoint leaves a
few hundred acknowledged letters that can never be revived, deleting
them one at a time is not a safeguard so much as an obstacle".

Two properties of the old shape are kept and are load-bearing:

* **One audit entry per letter**, never one for the batch —
  `webhook.dead_letter_discarded` carrying the event type and the
  endpoint name. "Those
  entries are what survives the deletion, and 'seventeen letters were
  deleted' would not be a record of anything."
* **Named ids only.** There is no discard-by-filter, and unlike
  acknowledge, an empty list is emphatically not "everything".

A malformed body is refused here, not defaulted, as it
now is on acknowledge and bulk replay too.

200.description: `discarded` can be smaller than `requested` — "when an id is not this tenant's, or was already gone. Reported rather than rounded up". An entirely unmatched set of ids is a 200 with `discarded: 0`, not a 404.

400.description: `invalid_request` — malformed JSON ("invalid JSON body"); `ids` omitted or empty ("ids is required and must name at least one letter; there is no discard-by-filter"); a platform token that named no `tenant_id`.

delete.description: The single-letter form of `/discard`, with the same one-audit-row-per-letter guarantee. Note it answers `200 {"discarded": true}` rather than the `204` its sibling `DELETE /api/v1/webhooks/{id}` uses.

parameters.name: id
parameters.description: Dead-letter id.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: Accepted and never read. Does nothing.

200.description: Deleted.

404.description: `not_found` — "no such dead letter for this tenant", or the management API is disabled.

get.summary: What happened to recent notifications
get.description:
"Closes the obvious question an operator has when a receiver has been
down: what is queued, what gave up, and why".

Newest first.

`status` is only ever `pending` or `delivered`: a delivery that runs
out of attempts leaves this listing and becomes a dead letter in the
same transaction. Anything
that gave up is on `/api/v1/webhook/dead-letters`, not here.

The payload body is deliberately not in this listing; it is in the
dead-letter listing, where an operator actually needs it.

parameters.name: webhook_id
parameters.description: Narrow to one endpoint — "the useful default view once there are several". Omitted means every endpoint.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: Omitted is 50; anything above 200 becomes 200; 0 or negative becomes 1. There is no cursor and no total — this is a tail, not a page.

200.description: Recent deliveries, newest first.

post.summary: Retry a batch of deliveries
post.description:
The bulk replay. Two quite different stores sit behind one word:

* `status: "exhausted"` (the default) revives **dead letters**. "the
  word is kept because it is what an operator means, and what their
  scripts already send", even though no queued
  delivery can be in that state any more. The letters are not deleted
  by a revival — "a revived event has been re-attempted, not received" —
  they clear when the delivery actually lands.
* `status: "delivered"` re-sends from the **live queue**, "for a
  receiver that accepted events and then lost them".

Bounded at 500 per call:
"without one, a single call after a long outage could put tens of
thousands of requests on the wire at once and take out the receiver a
second time." `more_may_remain` is true when exactly 500 were requeued, so a caller
knows to come back.

Omission semantics:

* The **whole body may be absent** — no bytes at all — and the request
  takes every default below, which is every exhausted delivery for the
  tenant, up to 500. A body that is **present and cannot be read** —
  malformed JSON, a wrong type, a content type other than JSON, or an
  unknown key — is a 400 and replays nothing. It used to be read as
  absent, so a typo in a filter replayed everything.
* `status` omitted → `"exhausted"`.
* `webhook_id` omitted → every endpoint.
* `since` omitted → all history.
* `ids` omitted is the same as `[]`; empty means "everything matching
  the filters", non-empty means exactly those letters.

An audit row (`webhook.replayed`, detail `requeued=<n>`) is written only
when something was requeued.

200.description: How many were requeued, and whether the cap was hit.

post.summary: Try one delivery again
post.description:
Takes an id from **either** list. "An operator reading the dead-letter list should not have to know that it is a different table from the delivery log, and the ids cannot collide, so try the queue first and then the dead letters". A queued delivery that is still `pending` is not requeued — "a delivery already in flight must not have its schedule reset underneath the worker" — and it is not a dead letter either, so the answer is 404.
No request body is read at all.

parameters.name: id
parameters.description: A delivery id or a dead-letter id.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: Accepted and never read. Does nothing.

200.description: Requeued. `requeued` is 1 in practice — either path requeues exactly one.

404.description: `not_found` — "no such replayable delivery for this tenant; one still pending, or already revived, is queued already". Also covers a dead letter whose endpoint has been deleted: "A letter for a deleted endpoint cannot be revived — there is nowhere to send it — and is skipped rather than counted". And the management-API-disabled 404.

get.summary: The tenant's notification endpoints
get.description:
Lists the endpoints this tenant's security events are sent to. Reading
this is how an operator answers "is anyone actually being told", which
is why either webhook scope satisfies it — "a key trusted to change a
thing is trusted to see it".

The secret is never returned by any operation in this group: "it exists
to be verified against, not read back".

Not paginated, and it does not need to be: a tenant may hold at most
10 endpoints. The `limit` query parameter is accepted and never read.
It does nothing.

x-auth.tenant-key: require_any_scope_if_restricted(&[SCOPE_WEBHOOKS_READ, SCOPE_WEBHOOKS_WRITE]) — management.rs. A key with no scopes at all is unrestricted (management.rs); a key that declares scopes must hold `webhooks:read` or `webhooks:write`.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: ACCEPTED AND IGNORED — see `GET /api/v1/apps`. Nothing here reads `limit`, and an unknown query parameter is not an error, so a non-integer value is not refused either. The full list is always returned.

200.description: The endpoints, oldest first.

post.summary: Add a notification endpoint
post.description:
Registers a destination for this tenant's events. Audited as
`webhook.endpoint_created` at **warning** severity, because "an attacker
who reached the Management API would add one before doing anything
else".

Tenant selection comes from the **request body** here (`tenant_id`),
not the query string — unlike GET and DELETE on
`/api/v1/webhooks/{id}`, which read it from the query.

Field-by-field behaviour when a field is omitted:

* `url` — **required**. Absent means the body is refused with a flat
  `invalid_request` / "invalid JSON body"; it does not name the missing
  field.
* `secret` — **required on create**. Minimum 16 characters. Supplied by
  the caller rather than generated so it can be put in the receiver's
  config first.
* `name` — optional; absent becomes the literal string `"default"`.
* `events` — absent is read as `[]`, and `[]` is then refused:
  "subscribe to at least one event". Absent and empty are the same thing here.
* `enabled` — **accepted and ignored.** A new endpoint is always
  created enabled, and the reply says `"enabled": true`. Posting `{"enabled": false}` creates an enabled
  endpoint.
* `max_deliveries_per_minute` — absent means the default 60. `0` is the
  explicit spelling for unlimited — absent and `0` are deliberately
  *different*, "because JSON `null` is indistinguishable from an omitted
  field and omitting it should mean 'the default', not 'turn the
  protection off'". Negative is refused.
* `disable_after_dead_letters` — absent means the default 100. `0`
  means never disable automatically. Negative is refused.

Unknown body fields are refused with the same
"invalid JSON body".

The 10-endpoint cap is enforced as the endpoint is stored, not by a
count read beforehand:
"Reading the count here first and deciding on it is what let two
simultaneous requests both see room and both take it".

x-auth.tenant-key: require_scope_if_restricted(SCOPE_WEBHOOKS_WRITE) — management.rs. Unscoped keys keep the authority they have always had; a scoped key needs `webhooks:write` (see the reasoning at management.rs).

201.description:
Created. Note this shape is **not** the same as the one `GET`
returns: it echoes the request rather than re-reading the row, and
so omits `disabled_reason` / `disabled_at` / `disabled_by`.

400.description:
`invalid_request` — malformed JSON, a missing required field or an
unknown one ("invalid JSON body"); `secret` shorter than 16 characters; no
`secret`; an event name outside `WebhookEventName`; empty `events`;
a negative `max_deliveries_per_minute` or
`disable_after_dead_letters`; a URL the SSRF guard refuses
("destination refused: …"); a platform token
that named no `tenant_id`.

`limit_reached` — the tenant already holds 10 endpoints
(message "a tenant may have at most 10 endpoints").

Also reached, and arguably wrongly, when the tenant data key cannot
be used to encrypt the secret: that failure surfaces as
`invalid_request` / "delivery failed: could not encrypt the
secret: …".

503.description: `contended` — repeatedly lost the race for a numbered endpoint slot. "503, not 400: the request is fine and would succeed on its own. This is the server saying it lost a race with itself". Retried 10 times internally first.

parameters.name: id
parameters.description: Endpoint id. A value that is not a UUID is rejected with a plain-text 400, not the JSON error shape — and only after authentication, which is checked first.

get.summary: One notification endpoint
get.description: Fetches a single endpoint. Never returns the secret. This is the only shape that reports the disable provenance — `disabled_reason`, `disabled_at`, `disabled_by` — which answers "who turned it off, and why".

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: Accepted and never read. Does nothing.

200.description: The endpoint.

404.description: `not_found` — "no such endpoint for this tenant", or "the management API is disabled" when `MANAGEMENT_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN` is unset. The two share a status and an error code and are distinguished only by `message`.

put.description:
A **full replace**, not a patch, and the omission semantics are the
trap:

* `tenant_id` comes from the **body** on this operation, where `GET` and `DELETE` on the same path take
  it from the query string.
* `name` omitted **renames the endpoint to `"default"`** — the
  same rule as create, where it is a sensible
  default and here is a silent rename.
* `url` is required, as on create; absent is refused as "invalid JSON body".
* `secret` omitted **keeps the stored one** — with `enabled`, one of
  the two fields where absent means "leave it alone". Supplied, it must still be ≥ 16 characters and is
  re-encrypted.
* `events` is required and non-empty, exactly as on create.
* `enabled` omitted keeps the stored value: absent means "leave it as
  it is", not "switch it on".
* `max_deliveries_per_minute` and `disable_after_dead_letters` omitted
  **reset to the defaults** 60 and 100, exactly as on create.

Only an enabled→disabled or disabled→enabled *transition* is audited,
not every save: "An update that leaves the endpoint on says nothing an
operator will later go looking for". The
transition is written as a second step, because a settings replace
deliberately does not touch the disable provenance (`disabled_reason`,
`disabled_at`, `disabled_by`).

200.description: Updated. Echoes the request, so — like the create reply — it omits `disabled_reason` / `disabled_at` / `disabled_by`. `enabled` is the resolved value, read from the pre-update row rather than re-fetched.

400.description: `invalid_request` — the create validation list minus "a secret is required", plus any failure while saving the new settings — a newly supplied secret that cannot be encrypted, or the write itself failing, database errors included — all answered with 400 rather than 500. Two failures are not 400: an endpoint that cannot be read is a 404, and a failed enable/disable step after the settings were saved is a 500 (see those responses).

404.description: `not_found` — "no such endpoint for this tenant". Also returned when the endpoint cannot be read for any reason — a database error on that read is reported as a missing endpoint.

500.description: `server_error` — the settings write landed but the follow-up enable/disable write, which carries the provenance, did not. "the state is genuinely partial: say so and let the caller retry, rather than paper over it". The audit row is *not* written in this case.

delete.description: Removes the endpoint and, by cascade, its queued deliveries. Audited as `webhook.endpoint_deleted` at warning severity — and the audit row is the only thing that survives: "deleting the row takes the endpoint, its deliveries and its dead letters with it, so without this entry there would be nothing left to say the tenant was ever being told about anything". The endpoint's name is read *before* the delete for exactly that reason; if the name cannot be read it falls back to the id string.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: Accepted and never read. Does nothing.

404.description: `not_found` — "no such endpoint for this tenant", or the management API is disabled.

post.summary: Rotate a tenant's token-signing key
post.description:
Mints a new RS256 keypair for the tenant, retires the previous one, and
bumps the tenant's keyring cache epoch — all in one transaction, so no
node can end up signing with a key this call has just retired.

**Signing keys, not API keys.** `/api/v1/tenants/{tenant_id}/keys` is the
API-key collection; this is one segment further on and means the other kind
of key entirely. The response says `signing_key` for the same reason.

**Not destructive.** The previous key is retired, not deleted, and stays in
the JWKS for its verification window, so every token already issued keeps
verifying. The one thing to avoid is rotating twice in quick succession:
the second call retires a key that tokens minted seconds earlier name.

Until this endpoint the only way to roll a tenant's keypair was
`admin-cli rotate-keys`, which needs a shell on the host.

**Auth:** platform (naming a tenant), an unscoped tenant key, or a key
holding `tenant:write` — a tenant-level configuration
change with no destructive half, so it rides the tenant-write scope rather
than adding one of its own.

**Audit:** `signing_key.rotated` at **warning**, carrying the new `kid`,
which is public and is what lines the trail up against tokens in the wild.

201.description: Rotated. The private key is never returned.

409.description: `rotation_too_soon` — a workspace's own API key already rotated this key in the last hour. A workspace key may rotate it once an hour; the platform credential is not limited. Nothing changes.

503.description: `unavailable` — the audit trail could not be read to check when the signing key was last rotated. Nothing changes; try again.

post.summary: Issue a new client secret while the old one still works
post.description:
The gap this closes: a machine client's secret could previously only be replaced by deleting and recreating the client, which changes the `client_id` and so requires every consumer to be reconfigured at the same moment. That makes routine credential hygiene an outage, so it does not happen — which is the actual security problem.

Two secrets are live at once. The new one is returned here, once; the old one keeps authenticating until `previous_secret_expires_at`, after which it stops. Retire it early with `/retire-secret` once every consumer has moved.

**Audit:** `client_secret.rotated` (warning), carrying the overlap.

auth.require_scope_if_restricted(apps:write)

parameters.description: Required when using the platform token.

requestBody.description: Optional. Absent or empty means the default overlap; a body that is present and cannot be read is a 400 and rotates nothing — see `SecretRotateRequest`. `tenant_id` goes in the query, never here.

200.description: Rotated. The new secret is in the body and is never shown again.

400.description: `invalid_request`: invalid JSON body — including a `tenant_id` sent in the body — or `overlap_hours` outside 1..720.

500.description: `server_error`: the new secret could not be hashed.

post.summary: End the overlap early, once every consumer has the new secret
post.description:
Stops the previous secret authenticating immediately, rather than waiting for `previous_secret_expires_at`. The point of rotation is that the window exists; the point of this is that it does not have to be waited out once it is no longer needed.

**Idempotent.** A client with no rotation window open is a 204, not a 404: the caller asked for the outgoing secret to be dead, and it is.

post.summary: Mint a successor key and give this one a deadline
post.description:
Mint-and-revoke already allowed two live keys. What was missing was the **deadline**: without one the overlap lasted until somebody remembered to revoke, which is why a key that should have been replaced last quarter is still in a CI variable.

The successor inherits the predecessor's name and scopes; the raw key is returned once and is not retrievable afterwards.

**A live key that names no scopes is refused with 409**, and nothing
changes: its successor would inherit the empty list, which is minting
an unscoped key by another route. Such a key keeps working until it is
revoked; replace it by minting a key with the scopes it needs, then revoking
it.

**Platform-only**, like every other operation on this collection — a tenant key that could mint its own successor would be a tenant key that never expires. Note this is the *key's* own id in the path, not the tenant's signing key: `/tenants/{tenant_id}/keys/rotate` is a different endpoint entirely, and putting this one under the key id keeps the router and the caller from confusing them.

**Audit:** `api_key.rotated` (warning), carrying the replaced id, its successor's id and the overlap.

Registers an API that clients may request tokens **for**. The `identifier` becomes the `aud` claim.

**Not an upsert.** A repeat is a 409, never a silent rebind: changing what an identifier points at would change what every token already carrying it is addressed to.

**Audit:** `resource_server.created` (warning). Whoever can write this table decides what this server will mint tokens for, so the identifier is in the row.

Stops new tokens being addressed to it. Tokens already carrying it keep verifying — they are signed, and nothing consults this table at verification time — which is the only thing deletion can honestly promise. Its scope definitions go with it.

**Audit:** `resource_server.deleted` (warning).

Defines a scope for one audience, or — with `resource_server_id` omitted — for the tenant at large.

What it buys: the consent screen can show the description instead of the raw string, and a token requested for an audience is narrowed to the scopes that audience defines. Narrowing only: a client cannot reach a scope its own allow-list lacks by naming an API that defines it.

put.summary: Set or clear the monthly-active-user soft cap
put.description:
**Soft**, and the word is load-bearing: passing this limit is announced, never enforced. Nothing is denied, no login fails, no user notices. A cap that could refuse a sign-in would put a billing table on the authentication path — the same mistake the recording of these numbers was written to avoid, made deliberately instead of by accident.

What happens when a tenant passes it: one `usage.soft_cap_exceeded` audit row (warning) at the crossing, and `over_soft_cap: true` on `GET /api/v1/usage`. Once per crossing, not once per login — raising the cap re-arms it, which is the behaviour an operator wants.

**Auth:** `tenant:write`, not a new `usage:write`. The *numbers* are recorded by the act of somebody signing in and nothing may write them through an API; a cap is an ordinary tenant setting that changes what gets said, never what gets counted or allowed.

**Audit:** `usage.soft_cap_set` (info) — because "why did we stop hearing about this tenant" should be answerable.

200.description: The cap as stored.

400.description: `invalid_request`: invalid JSON, an unknown field, or a cap of zero or less.

404.description: `not_found`: no such tenant.

get.summary: Which plan this tenant is on, and why
get.description:
The plan in force, where it comes from, and the subscription that pays for it — what a customer would see on their own billing page, and nothing more. **No billing-provider identifiers**: no customer, subscription, item or price ids. Buying and changing a plan happen in the tenant console (`/admin/billing`), where an owner is signed in; this endpoint only reads.

`plan` is the plan in force. `source` says why: `override` when the platform operator has set one (a comped account, an agreement — it wins whatever the subscription says), `subscription` when a subscription in force pays for it, `none` when nothing does and the tenant is on FREE.

A subscription is in force while its status is `active`, `trialing` or `past_due` (Stripe is still retrying the card); anything else — `canceled`, `unpaid`, `incomplete`, `incomplete_expired`, `paused` — leaves the tenant on FREE. An ended subscription is still returned, with `in_force: false`, so its history is visible.

Read from what the billing webhook last wrote, never from the provider, so it answers the same when billing is switched off for the deployment (`billing_enabled: false`).

**Auth:** `tenant:read`.
get.x-auth:
auth.tenant_scope(q.tenant_id)
auth.require_scope_if_restricted(SCOPE_TENANT_READ)   // "tenant:read"

Not a new `billing:read`: the plan already rides on every tenant read, and what
this adds is why. Nothing here is a credential or a capability.

200.description: The plan in force, its source, and the subscription if there has been one.

get.summary: How long sign-ins last for this tenant
get.description:
Reports the **configured** value and the **effective** one, which are different questions. `session_ttl_seconds: null` means nobody has set one — the tenant still has a lifetime, the deployment default. An endpoint that returned only the stored setting would answer "no session lifetime" for every tenant that never chose one, which is true of the setting and false of the system.

The bounds are returned alongside so a caller does not have to carry its own copy of them.

**Auth:** `tenant:read`.

auth.tenant_scope(None)
auth.require_scope_if_restricted(tenant:read)

put.summary: Set or clear this tenant's session lifetime
put.description:
Sets how long a sign-in lasts here; `null` restores the deployment default.

**Shortening it signs people out on their next request.** The lifetime is applied when a cookie is verified, not baked into the cookie when it is minted — so a tenant that shortens the window is answering "sign everyone out sooner", and gets that. A TTL carried inside each cookie would let every session already issued run to the old length, which would look like the change worked and would not have.

Out-of-range values are **refused**, not clamped. The same bounds are enforced by the database and again when the value is read, because a value stored some other way must not become a session that outlives the reason it was issued.

**Auth:** `tenant:write`.

**Audit:** `tenant.session_lifetime_set` (info) — "why did everyone get logged out on Tuesday" is otherwise unanswerable, because expired sessions simply stop verifying and leave no event.

200.description: The lifetime as stored, and what it resolves to.

get.summary: The SMS second factor's switch, whether the plan includes it, and this month's texts
get.description:
Text-message codes as a second factor: whether the tenant has switched them on, whether its plan includes them (TEAM and BUSINESS do), whether this deployment can send a text at all, and how many it has sent today and this month.

SMS is included in the paid plans and not billed per message, so the counts are here to make the cost visible. `sent_*` counts every text the server handed to the provider; `accepted_this_month` counts the ones the provider took.

`offered` is the answer a person setting it up gets: the switch **and** the plan. A tenant downgraded with the switch on reads `sms_factor_enabled: true` and `offered: false` — the switch is kept as set, so an upgrade restores it.

**Auth:** `tenant:read`.

put.summary: Turn the SMS second factor on or off
put.description:
**On needs a plan that includes SMS** — TEAM or BUSINESS. The plan is read from the database at the write, not from any cache, so an upgrade applies at the next request and so does a downgrade. A FREE tenant is refused with `403 forbidden` and a message naming the plans that include it. Where plans are not enforced every tenant the operator made may switch it on, and a tenant that self-service sign-up made may only once the operator has set its `plan_override` to TEAM or BUSINESS; until then it is refused with `403 forbidden` and a message that says so.

**Off is always allowed**, on any plan, and removes nobody's factor: it stops new enrolments, and at sign-in withdraws SMS from every account that has another way in while keeping it for the accounts it is the only way into, who are asked to add another factor.

Codes go to US and Canadian numbers only. SMS never satisfies `mfa_policy: "passkey"`.

**Auth:** `tenant:write`.

**Audit:** `tenant.mfa_sms_factor_changed` (warning), with the plan the change was judged against.

post.description:
A principal a machine client acts as, so that what a machine did is
attributable to something other than a person's account. Before this endpoint
one could only be made with SQL: nothing else creates them.

**Under `users:write`, not `apps:write`.** This creates a *principal*, and the
fact that a machine will act as it does not make it a client. An operator who
may mint clients but not people should not be able to mint people by calling
them robots.

**It cannot become a login.** It is created with no password — the
server's existing "cannot authenticate by password" marker — and the
database enforces that with a constraint, so the state holds against every
writer and not just this endpoint.

**Audit:** `service_account.created` (info), carrying the name.

Issue #6. Reads the app's registration and says what it will do before a real person finds out. It reports whether the app is switched on; whether a refresh token is issued (and so whether a session outlives an access token); whether `openid` is allowed; its redirect addresses (plain http, an address on the developer's own machine, two that differ only by a trailing slash); whether a post-logout address is registered; and its back-channel logout address, held to the rule it was registered under.

**Read-only, and from the registration alone.** It sends nothing to the app. Whether recent token requests failed to authenticate is not reported, because nothing records a failed client authentication.

put.description:
Separate from creating the client, so an existing deployment can adopt a
principal without re-registering. Re-registering changes the `client_id` and
forces every consumer to be reconfigured at one moment — the same outage that
made `/rotate-secret` worth building.

**PUT, and the body is the whole state.** An absent or `null`
`service_account_id` UNBINDS; there is no separate DELETE, and `{}` clears the
binding. A body is required, though: none at all is a 400. Sending the same id twice is a no-op rather than an error.

**One answer for two failures.** "No such client here" and "that id is not a
service account of this tenant" both return the same 400. They are both the
caller naming something that is not theirs, and telling them apart would
confirm which ids exist.

the principal — or its absence, so an unbind is as visible as a bind.

get.summary: List and filter a tenant's users
get.description:
The tenant directory, paged. `GET /api/v1/users?username=` beside this stays
an **exact** lookup that returns one person with their factor status; this
returns many, with less about each.

`q` matches username or email **case-insensitively, by substring**. Absent or
empty lists everyone. The match is deliberately loose: an administrator has a
fragment of an address, not an exact handle, and an exact-match search reads
as "this user does not exist".

**Paged, not capped.** A cap truncates silently and looks identical to a
tenant that simply has fewer users, which is how somebody concludes an
account was deleted. `total` counts every match so a caller can say
"26-50 of 4,312". `per_page` is fixed at 25 and is not a parameter - a page
size the caller chooses is a page size the caller sets to ten thousand.

Requires `users:read`. The action scopes (`users:reset_mfa`,
`users:revoke_sessions`) are **not** accepted, unlike on the exact lookup:
they are allowed there because a reset needs a user id and that lookup is the
only way to get one, which does not extend to paging through a roster.

Every call is audited as `user.directory_read` with the query, how many came
back and the total - the same event the tenant console emits for the same
read, because it is the same read. `q=@` returns everyone with an address, so
paging this endpoint is how anyone holding the scope reads an entire tenant.

parameters.name: q
parameters.description: Substring of a username or email. Absent lists everyone.

parameters.name: page
parameters.description: 1-based. Out-of-range pages return an empty list, not an error.

parameters.name: tenant_id
parameters.description: Required for a platform token; ignored for a tenant-scoped key.

200.description: Matches, capped at 25.

400.description: `invalid_request` - malformed query parameters.

post.summary: Deactivate or reactivate many accounts in one call
post.description:
**One call, one statement.** The point of this endpoint is that a client
forwards a single request rather than looping: the dashboard's webhook bulk
route walks the caller's ids and issues one upstream write per id, and a
request naming the same id 2000 times once produced 2000 writes. Here the ids
are deduplicated and the change is a single database statement.

* `action` is `"deactivate"` or `"reactivate"`. Deliberately not a boolean:
  `{"active": false}` is one typo from meaning its opposite, and this is the
  endpoint where a typo lands on fifty accounts.
* `reason` is **required**, as on the single-account routes. It is what the
  audit trail records.
* At most **50** accounts, counted *after* deduplication - a request naming
  one account fifty-one times is one write and is not refused.
* Deactivating revokes every named account's sessions at **one** instant, so
  the trail cannot show them straggling across a second.

Ids naming nobody in the tenant are returned in `not_found` rather than
failing the batch: a stale id in a pasted list is the ordinary case, and
refusing the whole request would make an operator unpick it by hand.

Every account gets its **own** audit rows - `user.deactivated` or
`user.reactivated`, plus `sessions.revoked` on a deactivation. A single
"bulk action" row would be unreadable as evidence about any one person.

**Clearing second factors is deliberately not offered in bulk.** That is a
backdoor: separately scoped, audited at warning severity, and requiring a
written reason per account precisely so each use is deliberate. Disarming
fifty accounts on one click would be the most dangerous route in the product.

200.description: The batch was applied; the body says what landed.

400.description: `invalid_request` - "invalid JSON body" (malformed, a content type other than JSON, or an unknown field), unknown action, missing reason, empty list, or more than 50 distinct accounts.

409.description: `conflict` — the batch would switch off every owner of the tenant who can sign in. Refused as a whole: nothing in it is written.

post.summary: Invite somebody to create their own account
post.description:
The other half of `POST /api/v1/users`. That endpoint takes a password an
operator chose, and the only way it reaches the person it belongs to is for
the operator to tell them — from which moment it is a credential two
people know, repaired only if the user later changes it.

This mails a single-use link instead. The invitee chooses a password nobody
else ever sees, and the address is marked verified on arrival, because
opening a link sent to an address is what proving control of it means.

**The same machinery the console uses to invite an administrator**, one step
short: only the token's SHA-256 is stored, it is spent by a single
atomic write, so it works once, it expires in 72 hours, and it
is never returned to the caller — an operator who could read the link could
accept it themselves and create an account bearing somebody else's address.

**Grants no role.** These invitations carry no role, which means
"create the account, grant nothing". Administrator seats are capped where
a role is granted, which this path never reaches, so an end-user invitation neither consumes a seat nor can be refused for want
of one.

**Refused for a suspended tenant.** A suspended tenant does not resolve, so
the link would 404 for whoever opened it — a dead link with no explanation
is worse than a 409 the operator can read. Lift the suspension and send it
again; one issued now would sit unusable and expire.

**Refused for an address that already has an account.** An email address is
unique within a tenant, so an invitation to an address somebody
already holds cannot be accepted under a new username — and by the time
acceptance runs into that, the token is spent. Refusing here tells the operator at the
moment they can still act. Acceptance also recognises the address, so the
narrow race where an account appears between issuing and accepting is a
redirect to sign-in rather than a dead end.

**Returning to the app.** Name the app with `client_id` and accepting ends there rather than on this server's sign-in page: a new account is signed in (through the workspace's second-factor rule) and sent to the app's `initiate_login_uri` with `iss`, OpenID Connect's third-party-initiated login. Only the app's own registered URI is ever followed, read when the invitation is accepted.

**Re-sending replaces.** A second invitation to the same address invalidates
the first, so there is never more than one working link per address.

**A tenant self-service sign-up made is held back**. Every invitation is a mail from the platform's own relay, so
such a tenant needs an owner whose email address is confirmed — refused
with 403 `owner_unconfirmed` until one is — and sends at most 20
invitations in any 24 hours until it is on a paid plan or the platform
operator overrides its plan: past that, 429 `invitation_quota_exhausted`,
with `Retry-After` the moment the oldest counted invitation leaves the
window. Either refusal writes and mails nothing. A tenant the operator made,
and the platform's own, are held to neither. The console's administrator
invitation is held to the same rule.

**Auth:** platform (naming a tenant), an unscoped tenant key, or a key
holding `users:write` — the same authority as creating
a user, because that is what this does; by which door is not a difference in
authority.

**Audit:** `user_invitation.sent` (info). Its own event type rather than
`tenant_invitation.sent` with a blank role: one hands somebody
administrative access to a tenant and the other creates an ordinary account,
and collapsing them would make the two indistinguishable in an alert.
post.x-auth:
auth.tenant_scope(req.tenant_id)
auth.require_scope_if_restricted(SCOPE_USERS_WRITE)   // "users:write"

The same authority as POST /api/v1/users, because this mints an account that
can sign in. Which door it came through is not a difference in authority.

202.description: Accepted. Nothing has been created — an account appears when somebody opens the link, and may never appear at all. `delivered` reports whether the mail went out; the invitation is live either way, so a caller told only "accepted" would wait for somebody who received nothing, and one told "failed" would re-send and invalidate a link that was in fact delivered.

400.description: `invalid_request` — invalid JSON body, an unknown field, an `email` that is not an address, or a `client_id` that cannot be returned to: "client_id names no app in this tenant" (another tenant's reads the same), "client_id names an app that is switched off, which could not sign anybody in", or "client_id names an app with no initiate_login_uri, so there is nowhere to return the invitee to; set one with PATCH /api/v1/apps/{client_id}"., or "client_id names an app whose initiate_login_uri no longer meets its rule ({why}); set it again with PATCH /api/v1/apps/{client_id}" — a stored address its redirect URIs have moved away from, which acceptance would not follow. Nothing is issued or mailed.

404.description: `not_found` — no such tenant, or the Management API is disabled on this deployment.

409.description: `conflict` — either this tenant is suspended (a suspended tenant does not resolve, so the link would 404 for whoever opened it), or a user with that email address already exists in it. The second is refused because an email address is unique within a tenant: such an invitation cannot be accepted under a new username, and by the time that is discovered the token has been spent. Or the platform operator has sent this address an owner invitation that is still live (`POST /api/v1/tenants/{tenant_id}/owner-invitations`): an end-user invitation does not replace it, and accepting it creates their account. Nothing is sent.

500.description: `server_error` — this deployment declares no tenant base host, so no invitation link can be built. A half-built URL would be mailed, look like a link, and resolve nowhere.

503.description: `temporarily_unavailable` — a tenant self-service sign-up made could not have its invitation allowance read. Refused rather than sent: a store that cannot answer has not said yes. Nothing was written or mailed.

get.summary: List the CAs a tenant accepts attested authenticators from
get.description:
Returns the policy alongside the list, because neither is actionable alone:
three CAs with attestation off pins nothing, and `required` with none is a
tenant whose users cannot register at all.

**Auth:** `tenant:read` or `tenant:write` when the key is scoped; a
tenant-scoped key may read its own.

200.description: The policy and its CAs.

post.summary: Register a CA whose authenticators this tenant will accept
post.description:
Adding a CA **widens** what counts as an acceptable authenticator under a
policy whose whole purpose is to be narrow, so it is audited at warning
(`passkey.attestation_ca_added`). A CA nobody remembers adding is how
"hardware keys only" quietly becomes "hardware keys, and whatever else
somebody vouched for".

This is also the prerequisite for turning the policy on at all: `required`
is refused with 409 until at least one CA exists.

**Auth:** `tenant:write` when the key is scoped.

201.description: Registered. The body carries the new CA's `id`.

400.description: A blank label, or a `cert_pem` that is not shaped like a PEM certificate. Refused here rather than at a user's registration, which is where it would otherwise surface.

parameters.name: ca_id
parameters.description: The CA to remove, from `listAttestationCas`.

delete.summary: Remove a CA from a tenant's attestation list
delete.description:
**Refused with 409 when it is the last CA and `passkey_attestation` is
`required`**, because the result would be a tenant whose users can register
nothing — and the operator who clicked remove would have no reason to connect
the two. Set the policy to `none` first, which is a decision rather than a
side effect.

This is the likelier of the two lockouts to be walked into: retiring a vendor
you no longer issue is an ordinary piece of housekeeping.

**Auth:** `tenant:write` when the key is scoped.

404.description: No such CA for this tenant.

409.description: The last CA under a `required` policy. The message names the order to do it in.

get.summary: Download everything a departing tenant may take with them
get.description:
GDPR portability, and the counterpart to `deleteTenant`. A tenant can be removed; this is how its owner leaves with their users, applications, connections and settings rather than only being erased.

**Nothing is exported by default.** An export policy names every tenant-scoped table with a disposition and a per-column action, and a test checks it against the live schema — so a migration that adds a table or column fails the build until somebody decides what it is. The failure mode of forgetting one is therefore a missing field, not a leaked credential.

**Secrets are redacted, and redaction happens in the statement.** A column holding a secret, a hash of a secret, a token, key material or ciphertext is selected as a literal `NULL`, so its value is never read out of the database. The key stays in the JSON deliberately: a customer planning a migration needs to see *that* their users have passwords and passkeys.

**Ephemeral tables are excluded and say so.** Authorization codes, one-time codes, WebAuthn challenges, sessions, pending enrolments and revocation markers are deleted with the tenant and never exported — every row expires in minutes or hours and all of it is credential material. `excluded` lists each one with its reason, so a reader comparing the export against the schema finds a decision for every absence.

**Capped, and truncation is reported.** At most 10,000 rows per table. Any table that hit the cap is named in `truncated`; an empty array means the export is complete. A short export that looked complete is the worst outcome available here.

**Platform scope**, matching `deleteTenant`: this is a copy of every user record a tenant holds, which is exactly the artefact a leaked tenant key must not be able to produce. Every call writes a `tenant.exported` audit entry recording who took a copy, how many rows, and whether it was complete.

200.description: The tenant's exportable data.

404.description: `not_found` — no such tenant.

get.summary: The tenant's SAML connections
get.description:
Every inbound SAML connection configured for this tenant, enabled or not.

A connection is the trust anchor for federated sign-in: it names the identity
provider, where its sign-on endpoint is, and the certificate whose signature will
be accepted.
get.x-auth:
auth.tenant_scope(...)
auth.require_scope(SCOPE_SAML_READ)    // "saml:read" — STRICT

Strict, like the mail pair and for a sharper reason. A SAML connection is the
trust anchor for a tenant's whole workforce: whoever can write one can point
federated sign-in at an identity provider they control and then sign in as
anybody in that tenant. The read side is strict too, because the row names the
provider, its endpoint and the certificate trusted — a map of how to impersonate
them convincingly.

A key holding saml:write is NOT thereby able to read, matching the mail pair.

200.description: OK

post.summary: Configure a SAML connection
post.description:
Registers an identity provider this tenant's users may sign in through.

The certificate is checked here rather than at sign-in, with the same loader
verification uses: a PEM that cannot be loaded, a sign-on URL that is not https,
a lifetime outside the permitted range, or an `acs_url` that is not an address this server answers on, is refused with 400 while the operator
is still looking at the form, rather than as a broken login afterwards.

A connection is disabled unless `enabled` says otherwise, and the platform's
per-tenant switch (`PUT /api/v1/tenants/{tenant_id}/saml`) must be on as well
before either sign-in route answers.

A connection may never trust this server's own identity provider: an
`idp_entity_id` on this deployment's names, or a certificate carrying a key this
deployment has published as an identity provider — any tenant's, including one
deleted after the key was recorded, and whatever name the certificate carries —
is refused with 400. A connection written some other way is refused at sign-in
for the same reasons.

See the note on saml:read.

409.description: `conflict` — this tenant already has a connection to that identity provider.

get.summary: May this tenant sign in with SAML, as a service provider?
get.description:
The platform's per-tenant switch for SAML phase 1: this tenant signing its people in through their own identity provider. Acting as an identity provider is a separate switch, `GET /api/v1/tenants/{tenant_id}/saml-idp`.

Separate from the `enabled` on each of the tenant's connections: this one is the operator saying "this customer may use SAML", and that one is the customer saying "this provider is live". Both must be on before a sign-in is possible.

Platform token only, and there is deliberately NO scope that grants it. The
switch exists because an operator decides who may reach a surface they have not
finished reviewing; a tenant able to answer that for themselves would not be the
switch that was asked for.

200.description: OK

put.summary: Turn SAML sign-in (phase 1) on or off for a tenant
put.description: Takes effect on the next request: the flag is read on every SAML sign-in request, before any XML is parsed, so a tenant switched off stops being able to start or finish a sign-in immediately. Sessions already established are untouched — they are sessions, not assertions.

200.description: OK

get.summary: May this tenant act as a SAML identity provider?
get.description:
The platform's per-tenant switch for SAML phase 2: whether this tenant may sign assertions for its registered service providers and publish IdP metadata.

Deliberately separate from `GET /api/v1/tenants/{tenant_id}/saml`, which is phase 1 (consuming assertions). Allowing one never allows the other.

able to answer that for themselves would not be the switch that was asked for.

200.description: OK

get.description:
Every application this tenant may sign users into with Proteles as the identity provider, enabled or not.

The acs_urls of each are the allowlist an assertion may be delivered to.

AppIdentity.description: The app a client is, for a mobile app: its Android package and signing-certificate fingerprints, its Apple app ID, or both; at least one is required. Each host among the client's redirect and post-logout URIs must vouch for it: `https://<host>/.well-known/assetlinks.json` with a `delegate_permission/common.handle_all_urls` statement for the package and one of the fingerprints, served as `application/json`; and `https://<host>/.well-known/apple-app-site-association` listing the app ID in `webcredentials.apps` (what `ASWebAuthenticationSession` requires for an `https` callback). Every field optional;
absent means "leave it alone".

**Unknown fields are refused**, so `{"redirectUris": [...]}` is a 400 rather
than a 200 that changed nothing — a caller moving a production callback
domain must not be told it worked when it did not. A body with no
recognised field at all is also a 400.

app_identity.description: Set (verified against the redirect URIs the client ends up with) or, with `null`, clear the client's app identity. ABSENT leaves it as it is; the redirects of a client that has one are verified again whenever they change.

backchannel_logout_uri.description: OIDC Back-Channel Logout 1.0 §2.2: where the app receives logout tokens when a session it was issued an ID token for ends. `null` stops it being told and clears `backchannel_logout_session_required` with it; ABSENT leaves it as it is. Held to the rule `POST` applies.

backchannel_logout_session_required.description: §2.2. ABSENT leaves it as it is, unless the URI is cleared, which clears it too. `true` needs a `backchannel_logout_uri`, set or kept.

initiate_login_uri.description: Where the app starts a sign-in a third party asks for (OIDC Dynamic Client Registration 1.0 §2), as on `POST`. `null` clears it; ABSENT leaves it as it is. Checked against the `redirect_uris` the app will have after this request, and a stored one is checked again when `redirect_uris` change: one left on an origin none of them has any more is refused, and the same request changes or clears it. An absolute `https` URI with no fragment and no user name or password, on the same origin (scheme, host and port) as one of the app's `redirect_uris`, without an `iss` parameter of its own (the server adds it), and at most 2048 bytes. `http` only on a loopback host — `localhost`, `127.0.0.1` or `[::1]` — exactly as a redirect URI may use it. Anything else is 400 `invalid_request`, "invalid initiate_login_uri: {why}".

If it contains `authorization_code`, the client must end up with at least one `redirect_uris` entry — checked against the *resulting* client, so adding the grant without URIs in the same request is a 400.

claim it. A mobile app registers a claimed `https` link (App Links,

ABSENT and `[]` are treated IDENTICALLY: both become

`refresh_token`, or the RFC 8628 device grant, sent as
`urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code` (the name discovery
advertises) or as `device_code`. The device grant is stored as `device_code`,
and a repeated value is stored once. Responses name it by the URN, as
`/register` does, so the list a response carries can be sent back
unchanged. Anything else is
400 `invalid_request`, "unsupported grant_type: {value}", naming the
value as sent. These are the values RFC 7591 registration at `/register`

The PUBLIC half of the key the client signs assertions with: an RSA public
key in PEM, labelled `PUBLIC KEY` (SPKI), `RSA PUBLIC KEY` (PKCS#1) or

REFUSED with any other method — a key nothing will ever consult

PARSED, not stored blindly: a PEM that cannot be read is a 400 here, while

reaches this server.
