Stable machine-readable slug. The values reachable on the operations
that answer with this body are exactly the eight below.

message.description: Human-readable sentence. Not stable; do not match on it.

detail.description: Only on a 400 whose `message` is "invalid JSON body": what about the body could not be read, as the parser reports it — the unknown field and the fields expected, the type that did not fit, a missing `Content-Type: application/json`. At most 300 characters, and it can quote what was sent. Not stable; for a person reading it, not for matching.

client_id.description: Only on `POST /api/v1/apps`, when the client was created and a later step of the same request failed — binding its `service_account_id`, or storing its `app_identity`, `backchannel_logout_uri` or `initiate_login_uri`. The client exists, `app.created` is in the trail, and this is its id: finish it with `PATCH /api/v1/apps/{client_id}`.

client_secret.description: Beside `client_id` there, for a confidential client that holds a secret: the secret minted for it, which is returned nowhere else.

next_cursor.description: Pass as `cursor` for the next page. `null` at the end of the list — null rather than absent, so a client can tell "the end" from "this server does not paginate". Opaque and sealed; its contents are not part of the contract.

AuditEventRecord.description: Rendered by the same code as each row line of `GET /api/v1/audit/export`, so the two cannot drift. The stored `id` is deliberately not exposed: it is a deployment-wide sequence, and two of them an hour apart would tell one tenant how many rows every other tenant wrote in between.

event_type.description: A fixed vocabulary. The webhook ones: `webhook.endpoint_created`, `webhook.endpoint_deleted`, `webhook.endpoint_enabled`, `webhook.endpoint_disabled`, `webhook.replayed`, `webhook.dead_lettered`, `webhook.dead_letters_acknowledged`, `webhook.dead_letter_discarded`, `webhook.dead_letters_purged`. Not all of them come from an operation: `webhook.dead_lettered` is written by the delivery worker when it gives up on a delivery, `webhook.endpoint_disabled` also when that worker switches off an endpoint that has lost too many events, and `webhook.dead_letters_purged` by the scheduled sweep that removes acknowledged dead letters past their retention.

severity.description: `warning` "marks the security-suspicious ones … so an audit consumer can filter for them". `critical` is the rung above it: somebody believes a credential that vouches for identity to third parties is in the wrong hands — today `saml_idp_key.revoked` alone.

actor_user_id.description: The subject — the resource owner this event concerns, not whoever caused it. See `caused_by_user_id` for the other end.

caused_by_user_id.description: The console member who performed the action, when one did. `null` for the whole authentication path, where nobody performed anything on anybody's behalf, and for actions taken by a platform operator or an API key — those are `asserted_operator` in `detail_json` and prose in `detail` respectively, because neither is a user of this tenant. Hashed into the row's leaf (`leaf_version` 3), so it cannot be edited after the fact without breaking the seal.

detail.description: Free-form `k=v` text, never secrets. May end with `asserted_operator=…` when a platform caller sent `X-Proteles-Operator`; only the server writes that key, and a caller cannot. `(rejected)` is the sentinel for a claim that was sent but unusable — "'nobody claimed anything' and 'somebody claimed something malformed' are different facts".

detail_json.description: The same event as JSON, as a **string** holding the stored bytes verbatim — never an embedded object. The seal hashes those bytes, so round-tripping them through JSON would let a re-serialiser reorder keys or rewrite whitespace and produce a value that fails to verify for a reason that is not tampering. Parse this rather than `detail`: `detail` is prose and is explicitly not a parsing target.

leaf_version.description: Which hashing rule covers this row, for a consumer that also verifies the sealed export.

ConnectionsConnection.description:
A configured connection. Identical shape in the 200 of the upsert
and in each element of the listing. No secret field ever appears.

in_use.description: Whether this connection works on the tenant's plan now: the enabled ones, oldest first, up to the plan's number of social logins. An enabled connection past that number is off — kept, and back when the plan allows it.

ConnectionsUpsertRequest.description: Unknown fields are refused: a 400 `invalid_request` "invalid JSON body", and nothing is done. An absent `enabled` means on, so a misspelling of it used to switch on a connection the caller was switching off.

tenant_id.description: Required with the platform token (400); must be the key's own tenant otherwise (403).

provider.description:
REQUIRED — omitting it fails the whole body as "invalid JSON body".
Must be one of the providers sign-in supports; anything else is 400
`invalid_request`.

client_id.description:
REQUIRED and non-blank: rejected when empty or only whitespace. The
provider's public client identifier; echoed back in the response and
in the listing.

client_secret.description:
REQUIRED. Note the asymmetry with the other two fields: only an empty
value is refused, not a blank one, so `""` is
refused but a single space is accepted and stored. Never echoed back,
by this endpoint or the listing; encrypted with the tenant's own data
key before storage.

redirect_uri.description:
REQUIRED. Must be this server's own callback for `provider` on a host of
the tenant: `{scheme}://{tenant host}/login/{provider}/callback`, where
the scheme is the issuer's and the host is one the server places on
this tenant — `<slug>.<base host>` (the base host itself for the
default tenant) or a verified custom domain — whether or not the
tenant is suspended. No query, fragment or userinfo; the port is not
compared. It is stored and sent to the provider as written, so it must
be written as a URL parser writes it back: no surrounding space, no `.`
segments, a lowercase host, no default port. Anything else is 400
`invalid_request`.

enabled.description:
ABSENT or `null` -> `true`. Note this is the opposite polarity
to `first_party` on app creation: here the PERMISSIVE value is the
default, so an upsert that omits `enabled` turns a previously disabled
connection back ON. There is no partial update — this is a full
replace, and every field must be resent.

previous_version.description: What was active before. 0 if the tenant had no data key yet.

notice.description: States that existing secrets are not re-encrypted — the opposite is the natural assumption and acting on it would be a mistake.

MailSettings.description:
A tenant's outbound relay. The SMTP password is absent from this schema and from every
response that uses it — not the value, and not a masked stand-in, because a `••••••` in a
JSON field is a value some client eventually sends back, and this one would be stored as
the password. `password_set` is what a form actually needs: it decides whether an empty
field means "keep the stored one" or "there is none".

configured.description: False when this tenant has no row and uses the platform relay.

using.description: Present only when `configured` is false — a description of the platform default.

username.description: Null for a relay that authorises by source address — a real configuration, not a half-filled form.

password_set.description: Whether a password is stored. The value itself is never returned.

from_address.description: Routinely differs from `username`: most shared hosts authenticate as a mailbox and let it send as an alias.

from_name.description: The name people see as the sender, beside `from_address`: `Proteles` in `From: Proteles <noreply@proteles.com>`. Sent as typed, quoted or encoded as the header needs, so a comma, a double quote or a non-ASCII name is fine. A name saved before the rule on `MailSettingsRequest.from_name`, and refused by it, is still returned here and left off the mail, which goes out from the address alone.

encryption.description: `none` is refused unless the host is loopback. There is no default: 587/STARTTLS and 465/implicit are both ordinary, so guessing from the port would be wrong about half the time, and wrong toward an unencrypted session carrying a password.

enabled.description: False falls back to the platform relay rather than stopping mail — switching a relay off means "not through this one", and reading it as "no mail at all" would silently break password recovery.

last_error.description: The relay's own words, truncated to 500 characters. Cleared by the next success.

password.description: Three readings, distinguishable on purpose. **Omitted** keeps the stored password — the same rule as a webhook secret. **`""`** clears it, which is the only way to move a relay from authenticated to anonymous without deleting the configuration and retyping it. **Anything else** replaces it. Validation sees the *effective* configuration, so an update that omits the password but names a username is not read as a username with no password.

from_name.description: The name people see as the sender, such as `Proteles`, not an address: a name containing `@`, `<` or `>`, a control character, a line break or a text-direction mark, one starting with a dot, or one over 100 characters is refused with a 400 `invalid_request` that says so. Trimmed before it is checked and stored. Sent as typed, quoted or encoded as the header needs, so a comma, a double quote or a non-ASCII name is fine. Omitted, null or blank sends from the address alone.

MailSettingsRequest.description: Unknown fields are refused: a 400 `invalid_request` "invalid JSON body", and nothing is done.

to.description: Where the test goes: a bare address — at most 254 bytes once trimmed, no whitespace or control character, and an addr-spec with nothing around it: no display name, angle brackets, comment or list, and no quoted local part, at a domain name with a dot, not an IP address or other bracketed literal. The rule every endpoint that takes an address applies; the address reported as tested is the one the relay was given.

MailTestRequest.description: Unknown fields are refused: a 400 `invalid_request` "invalid JSON body", and nothing is done.

MailTestResult.description:
Answered with 200 whether or not the relay accepted the message. A failed test is a
successful diagnosis: "535 authentication failed" is the entire value of this endpoint,
and burying it in a 502 with a generic message sends the operator to server logs they
cannot read.

via.description: Present when `sent` is true — which transport carried it.

error.description: Present when `sent` is false — the relay's own words, verbatim.

ManagementApiError.description: The uniform error body for the whole management API.

message.description: Human-readable. Not stable; do not match on it.

detail.description: Only on a 400 whose `message` is "invalid JSON body": what about the body could not be read, as the parser reports it — the unknown field and the fields expected, the type that did not fit, a missing `Content-Type: application/json`. At most 300 characters, and it can quote what was sent. Not stable; for a person reading it, not for matching.

identifier.description: The value that lands in a token's `aud`. Compared exactly — a trailing slash is a different audience.

tenant_id.description: Required when using the platform token.

identifier.description: An absolute URI with no fragment or whitespace, e.g. `https://billing.internal.example`. This is what a client passes as `resource` and what appears in `aud`.

tenant_scopes.description: Scopes that belong to no audience — `openid` and friends — which would otherwise be invisible here.

resource_server_id.description: Omit for a tenant-wide name. Must be a resource server this tenant owns.

name.description: A valid OAuth scope token: printable ASCII, no spaces, quotes or backslashes.

description.description: Required. A registry of names with no meanings is what this replaces.

resource_server_id.description: Null for a tenant-wide name such as `openid` or `profile`.

description.description: What the consent screen shows a human instead of the raw string.

overlap_hours.description: How long the outgoing secret keeps authenticating. Refused outside 1..720 rather than clamped — a caller asking for 10000 has a belief about the window, and silently giving them a different one is worse than a 400. Defaults to 168 (seven days).

SecretRotateRequest.description:
The body of both rotations, and optional: absent or empty (no bytes at all) means the default
overlap of 168 hours, and so does `{}`. A body that is present and cannot
be read — malformed JSON, a wrong type, a content type other than JSON, or
an unknown key — is a 400 `invalid_request` "invalid JSON body" and
rotates nothing. `tenant_id` is such a key: the app route reads it from
the query.

client_secret.description: The new secret, shown **once**. Same contract as app creation.

previous_secret_expires_at.description: After this the outgoing secret stops authenticating.

tenant_id.description: Required when using the platform token.

soft_cap.description: The limit, or null to remove it. Zero and negatives are refused: they read as "no access", which this setting cannot mean.

tenant_id.description: Platform credentials only; a tenant key is scoped to its own tenant.

session_ttl_seconds.description: Seconds, or null for the deployment default.

tenant_id.description: Platform credentials only; a tenant key is scoped to its own tenant.

enabled.description: Required: a PUT that switched SMS off because a field was misspelt would be a setting nobody chose.

SmsFactor.description: The SMS second factor at one tenant.

sms_factor_enabled.description: The tenant's switch, as set. A downgrade does not change it.

plan_includes_sms.description: Whether this tenant may switch SMS on: TEAM and BUSINESS may where the tenant is held to its plan, and every plan may where it is not (plans not enforced, or the platform's own tenant) — except that a tenant self-service sign-up made follows its plan either way, so where plans are not enforced it may only once the operator's `plan_override` is TEAM or BUSINESS.

offered.description: `sms_factor_enabled` and `plan_includes_sms`: whether a person here may set it up.

deliverable.description: Whether this deployment can send a text at all. `false` with no SMS provider configured, and then nobody can enrol whatever the switch says.

daily_limit.description: `SMS_TENANT_DAILY_LIMIT`: texts this tenant may send in a UTC day.

sent_today.description: Texts handed to the provider today (UTC). What the daily limit counts.

sent_this_month.description: Texts handed to the provider this calendar month (UTC).

accepted_this_month.description: Of those, the ones the provider accepted. The number closest to the bill.

TenantApiKeyCreateRequest.description:
Unknown fields are refused, and the reason is the security model: if
they were ignored, `{"scopez": ["audit:read"]}` would read as a body with
no `scopes`, "and the request that asked for least privilege is
answered with a key that has all of it — 201 and no hint".

Since 2026-10-01 a body with no `scopes` is refused as well, so that mistake
would be a 400 either way; refusing the unknown field names the real error.

scopes.description:
**Required, with at least one scope**. Omitting
it, or sending `[]`, is a 400 and mints nothing.

A key that names no scope passes every held-to-what-you-declare check and no
strict one, so it can do everything a tenant key can except the operations
behind a strict scope: `users:reset_mfa`, `users:revoke_sessions`,
`users:write` on bulk changes, deactivation and reactivation,
`domains:write`, `mail:read`, `mail:write`, `usage:read`, `saml:*` and
`saml-sp:*` (see `TenantApiKeyScope`). Keys minted that way before 2026-10-01
keep working, and are listed with `scopes: []`; none is minted any more, by
this route or by rotation (`rotateApiKey` answers 409 for one).

Duplicates are accepted; there is no cap on the array's length, only on its
contents.

TenantApiKeyCreated.description:
The **only** time the raw key is ever
available — only its SHA-256 is stored.

id.description: The key's id: what revocation and rotation take, and what a SAML service provider registration's audit rows written with this key name as `api_key_id`. Not secret.

api_key.description:
`mk_` followed by 32 OS-random bytes, base64url without
padding, so 43 characters after the prefix, 46 in total.

name.description: The name that was used, including the `"management key"` default.

scopes.description: Echoed back exactly as sent. Never empty: since 2026-10-01 a key with no scopes is not minted.

TenantApiKeyRevoked.description: Returned for a second revocation too.

TenantApiKeyScope.description:
The complete mintable set. A scope outside this list is refused at mint time, because under held-to-what-you-declare semantics a typo would otherwise produce a key that is bound but can never satisfy its binding — discovered as a 403 in production instead of a 400 in the operator's face.

**Two enforcement rules, and which applies is per *operation*, not purely per scope.** `x-scope-enforcement` below carries the machine-readable map, checked against the server on every pipeline.

* *held-to-what-you-declare* — an unscoped key passes; a scoped key is held to its list. Most reads also accept their write sibling, but not all: nothing that takes `users:read` accepts `users:write`, and `GET /tenant/session-lifetime` and `GET /saml/idp-keys` take `tenant:read` alone. Covers `tenant:*`, `apps:*`, `connections:*`, `resources:*`, `users:read`, `audit:read` and `webhooks:*`. The rule is not reserved for old operations: many added later are held too, and an unscoped key could call each of them from the day it shipped.
* *strict* — required outright, unscoped keys included. An unscoped key passes every held check, so under a held rule every unscoped key would have the operation; strict is for the ones too sensitive for that — clearing a user's factors, signing them out everywhere or cutting off their access, pointing a hostname at the tenant, the tenant's mail settings, its usage numbers, and SAML in either direction. Covers `domains:write`, `mail:read`, `mail:write`, `usage:read`, `saml:read`, `saml:write`, `saml-sp:read` and `saml-sp:write`; `saml-sp:write` is also what minting, promoting and revoking the identity-provider signing key take (since 2026-10-10), where `tenant:write` used to do. No strict write scope stands in for its read: a key holding `mail:write`, `saml:write` or `saml-sp:write` still needs the matching read scope to read.

**Three scopes are enforced both ways**, which is the part a per-scope reading gets wrong.

`users:write` is held on `POST /users`, `POST /users/invite` and the service-account route — creating a user is additive — and strict on `POST /users/bulk`, `POST /users/{id}/deactivate` and `POST /users/{id}/reactivate`, because denying somebody access to their account is not.

`users:reset_mfa` and `users:revoke_sessions` are strict on the operations they name, and *held* on `GET /users`, the lookup by `username`, which accepts any of them or `users:read`. So each doubles as a read grant for the user it is about to act on: a key scoped only to reset a factor can still look up whose factor it is. Classifying them strict-only misdescribes that route.

TenantApiKeySummary.description: Never the raw key, never the hash.

id.description: The identifier `DELETE .../keys/{key_id}` and `POST .../keys/{key_id}/rotate` take — the same `id` the mint response returns. Listed here too, so a key whose mint response is long gone can still be found and revoked.

scopes.description:
Typed as a free string array rather than the scope enum: these are
whatever was stored, and a key minted before a scope was retired
could carry a value no longer in `TenantApiKeyScope`.

revoked.description:
True once the key has been revoked. The
timestamp itself is never exposed, only the boolean.

TenantBranding.description:
Per-tenant look-and-feel for the hosted sign-in/consent pages and for
the SDK via `/.well-known/tenant-ui`.

**The read shape.** A field that was never set — or was cleared —
is *absent*, never present as `null`. The object itself is always
present, `{}` when nothing is configured.

The write shape is different and is a separate schema:
`TenantBrandingPatch`.

primary_color.description:
A CSS color for primary buttons/accents, e.g. "#1a7f37". Stored
unvalidated; the hosted pages sanitise it at render time
rather than at write time, so a
value that survives here can still be discarded on the page.

TenantBrandingPatch.description:
A **partial** change to a tenant's branding.

**Three states per field, and the difference is the point:**

* field **absent** → leave it alone;
* field present as **`null`** → clear it;
* a **string** → set it.

So `{"branding":{"app_name":"X"}}` on a tenant that has a logo and a
colour changes only the name, and `{"branding":{}}` is a no-op. It was
not always so: this used to be a whole-object replace, which is what
made `updateTenantBranding(id, {app_name})` silently erase the other
two.

**Unknown fields are refused**, as in the request object that carries it.
`{"branding":{"appName":"X"}}` is a 400 `invalid_request` and nothing
in the request takes effect — including any `mfa_policy` sent
alongside. A typo here is refused, not dropped.

app_name.description:
At most 100 characters, none of them a control character (a line
break, a tab, NUL): it is every hosted page's title and every mail's
subject. `null` clears it.

logo_uri.description: An absolute `https` URL of at most 2048 bytes. `null` clears it.

primary_color.description: A CSS color, e.g. "#1a7f37". `null` clears it.

TenantCreateRequest.description:
Unknown fields are refused, as on
the key-mint body: an unrecognised key is a 400 `invalid_request` "invalid
JSON body", and no tenant is created.

display_name.description:
Optional. **Absent and empty differ.** Absent → the display name
becomes the lowercased slug. Present as `""` → stored as the empty
string.

Write-only in practice: no endpoint in this group returns it.

owner_email.description: A contact address for whoever the tenant is held responsible to. Optional, and absent or blank is no contact; otherwise a bare address — at most 254 bytes once trimmed, no whitespace or control character, and an addr-spec with nothing around it: no display name, angle brackets, comment or list, and no quoted local part, at a domain name with a dot, not an IP address or other bracketed literal, the rule every endpoint that takes an address applies. Stored trimmed on the tenant row and in the `tenant.created` audit row; the server reads it nowhere else. It creates no account, grants nothing and sends no mail. To give the workspace an owner, send them an invitation: `POST /api/v1/tenants/{tenant_id}/owner-invitations`.

TenantDetail.description:
The `getTenant` body, also returned by
`PATCH`.

`plan` is the plan in force; `plan_subscribed` is what the billing provider says the customer pays for (`tenants.plan`); `plan_override` is the operator's, and wins when set.

issuer.description: The OpenID Connect issuer an application configures to sign this tenant's users in: the tenant's own origin, `<slug>.<base host>`, or the server's issuer for the default tenant. `null` on a deployment with no tenant base host. A verified custom domain is an issuer too, and is not listed here.

branding.description:
Always present as an object; `{}` when nothing is configured — an
unset field is omitted rather than sent as `null`, and a read failure
falls back to the empty object.

mfa_policy.description:
`optional` for a tenant that has never set one, so existing tenants
keep behaving exactly as before.

`passkey` is `required` narrowed to one factor: TOTP does not satisfy
it. A user holding only TOTP is still challenged for it at sign-in —
removing that would let a password alone reach the enrolment page —
and is then sent to register a passkey.

mfa_grace_days.description:
How long users who **predate** the requirement have to enrol,
measured from when the requirement began — not a fresh extension
from today. `0` (the default) means the requirement bites at once.

mfa_required_since.description:
RFC 3339. When the current requirement began. `null` both for a
tenant that requires nothing and for one that turned the requirement
on before this was recorded — deliberately not backfilled, since
"inventing a date would hand out a grace window nobody asked for".

mfa_grace_until.description:
RFC 3339. `mfa_required_since` plus `mfa_grace_days`, or `null` if the
policy is `optional`, `mfa_grace_days` is 0, or `mfa_required_since` is
unknown.

mfa_self_recovery_hours.description:
How long after a user proves their mailbox their second factors are
cleared, in hours. `null` — the default, and what every tenant that
predates this has — means the tenant does not offer self-service
recovery at all and a user who has lost every factor still needs an
operator.

Null rather than `0` or `false`, because off is the *absence* of the
setting: turning it off removes the setting rather than storing a
zero, so a
tenant that turned this on and off again is indistinguishable from
one that never asked.

A stored value that is not a positive integer reads as `null` here.
That is the direction a corrupt setting must fail in: it can only
withdraw the feature, never switch it on for a tenant that did not
ask for it.

passkey_attestation.description:
Whether this tenant demands an attestation chain when a passkey is
registered. `none` for every tenant that has not said otherwise.

**`required` is not "stricter passkeys", it is "hardware keys only".**
Synchronised authenticators — iCloud Keychain, Google Password Manager,
1Password — attest to no CA a tenant can register, so a tenant switching
this on is telling its users that the passkey already on their phone will
not be accepted. Coherent for an enterprise issuing YubiKeys; ruinous as a
default.

attestation_ca_count.description:
How many CAs back the policy above. Returned beside it because the two are
only meaningful together: `required` with a count of `0` is a tenant whose
users cannot register any credential at all, and the policy alone does not
show that. The API refuses to create that state (409), but a tenant can
reach it by other doors, and this is where an operator would see it.

max_members.description:
Maximum administrators this tenant may hold. `null` means no limit,
which is what every tenant has until one is set.

Lowering it below `member_count` removes nobody: the cap governs
admission, not tenure, so the tenant keeps its members and admits no
more until the count falls below the new number.

member_count.description:
How many the tenant holds now. Returned beside the cap because a cap
without a count cannot be acted on — "3" does not say whether a seat
is free.

owner_count.description: How many of those members are owners — whether anybody can open the workspace's console and hand out roles. A workspace made with `POST /api/v1/tenants` starts at 0; `POST /api/v1/tenants/{tenant_id}/owner-invitations` invites one. `null` when the members could not be read, rather than a 0 that would say there is no owner.

mfa_email_factor_enabled.description: Whether users in this tenant may arm a code mailed to their address as a second factor. Off unless the tenant turned it on. Always present, including when false: an operator reading these settings is deciding about a factor, and an absent key would read as "not a thing this server has" rather than "a thing you have not enabled". It does not satisfy `mfa_policy: "passkey"` — a mailed code is not phishing-resistant.

account_recovery_codes_enabled.description: Whether accounts in this tenant with no confirmed email address may hold a saved account-recovery code — shown once, kept offline, and spent at `/account/recover` to choose a new password. Off unless the tenant turned it on, and always present, for `mfa_email_factor_enabled`'s reason.

password_signup_enabled.description: Whether a person may make their own account in this tenant on its hosted sign-up page, with an address and a password. Off unless the tenant turned it on, and always present, for `mfa_email_factor_enabled`'s reason.

social_signup_enabled.description: Whether a first sign-in through one of this tenant's social connections makes an account. Off, a person who already has an account still signs in that way: by an identity already linked, or one linked on an address both sides verified. Off for a new tenant, and always present.

plan_override.description: The operator's override, or `null`. When set it is the plan in force.

seat_cap.description: What a new member grant is held to: the lower of the plan's cap (five on FREE and TEAM; none on BUSINESS, which sells seats; none on any plan where `plans_enforced` is false) and `max_members`. `null` when neither caps.

plans_enforced.description: Whether this tenant is held to its plan: the deployment enforces plans (`PLANS_ENFORCED`) and the tenant is not the platform's own (the default tenant, which no plan limits). `false`: the plan is recorded and shown, and limits nothing. `plan_binding` says which of the two it is.

plan_binding.description: Why the plan does or does not bind this tenant, in `plan::binding`'s order: `not_enforced` — the deployment does not enforce plans (`PLANS_ENFORCED` is off), checked first, for every tenant including the default one; `platform_tenant` — plans are enforced, and this is the platform's own (default) tenant, which no plan limits; `plan` — held to its plan. `not_enforced` and `platform_tenant` are the two reasons `plans_enforced` is false, and the only way to tell them apart: on the default tenant the boolean is false either way, so this is how an operator whose one tenant is the default reads whether `PLANS_ENFORCED` is on. Absent from a server before 2026-10-03.

TenantDomainAddRequest.description: Unknown fields are refused: any key but `domain` is a 400 `invalid_request` "invalid JSON body", and nothing is claimed.

domain.description:
The hostname to claim. Normalised before validation and storage: surrounding whitespace
trimmed, trailing dots stripped, ASCII-lowercased.

Then checked by a rule that is "hygiene, not a security control" —
deliberately conservative and not a general DNS-name validator. It
requires:
non-empty; total length ≤ 253; at least one `.`; no leading or
trailing `.`; no `..`; and for every label: non-empty, ≤ 63
characters, no leading or trailing `-`, and only ASCII alphanumerics
and `-`.

So these are all refused: `localhost` (no dot),
`*.acme.com`, `https://login.acme.com`, `login.acme.com/path`,
`login.acme.com:8443`, `.acme.com`, `acme..com`, `-acme.com`,
`acme-.com`. Non-ASCII is refused; submit punycode (`xn--…`).

TenantDomainClaim.description:
How a claim is reported back, including what to publish to finish
it. Returned by both
the claim and the list endpoints.

verified.description:
`true` exactly when `verified_at` is set. While false, host
resolution refuses to match the claim, so the hostname resolves
nothing.

verified_at.description:
RFC 3339. Kept as a date rather than a boolean "so an operator can
see how stale the proof is" — a verified row outlives the DNS
control it recorded.

TenantDomainVerified.description:
The verify success body. Note it is *not*
`TenantDomainClaim` — a caller that wants `verified_at` or the challenge
after proving must re-list.

domain.description: The normalised form the server used, not necessarily what was sent.

TenantStatus.description:
One of `active`, `suspended` or `deleted`; the default is
`active`. `PUT /api/v1/tenants/{tenant_id}/status` moves a tenant
between `active` and `suspended`, and self-service sign-up suspends a
tenant it could not finish provisioning. Nothing writes `deleted`: the
stored status allows it, but `DELETE /api/v1/tenants/{tenant_id}`
removes the tenant rather than marking it. Only an `active`
tenant is served; any other status is refused at host resolution.

previous_status.description: What it was before this call. Returned so the caller can tell a real transition from a repeat — a second suspend replaced nothing.

status.description: `deleted` is refused, though the stored status can hold it — see the operation description.

reason.description: Free text, recorded in the audit detail. Optional: an operator acting on an obvious abuse report should not be blocked by a form field, and a required reason mostly produces the word "abuse".

TenantStatusRequest.description: Unknown fields are refused: a 400 `invalid_request` "invalid JSON body", and nothing is done.

TenantSummary.description:
What `POST /api/v1/tenants` and `GET /api/v1/tenants` return —
three fields.
`display_name` is deliberately absent; see `TenantCreateRequest`.

TenantUpdateRequest.description:
Every field optional; `{}` is a valid no-op. Unknown fields are
refused, as in the `branding` object inside it, so `{"brandnig": {...}}` is a 400
`invalid_request` "invalid JSON body" and nothing sent with it takes
effect.

branding.description:
A partial change: absent leaves a sub-field alone, `null` clears it, a
string sets it. See `TenantBrandingPatch` — in particular that an
unrecognised key inside this object fails the whole request, as one in
the enclosing object does.

mfa_policy.description:
Anything outside the enum is a 400, never a silent ignore — "a typo
must not leave an operator believing they have turned MFA on when
they have not". Matching is case-sensitive:
`"Required"` is refused.

`passkey` requires specifically a passkey. Moving between `required`
and `passkey` does **not** restart the rollout window: the requirement
has been running the whole time, and re-stamping it would push every
user's deadline out again.

mfa_grace_days.description:
At most 730;
out of range is 400. Two years is
"well past any real migration; the cap exists so a typo like `36500`
cannot turn a required policy into a permanently optional one while
still reading as 'required' on every screen".

The window is always measured from when the requirement began, so
changing it re-cuts the same window rather than opening a new one.

mfa_self_recovery_hours.description:
Turn self-service second-factor recovery on, change its delay, or
turn it off. **Three-state**, like `max_self_registered_clients`:

* field **absent** → leave the setting alone;
* `null` → turn the feature off;
* an integer → turn it on with that delay, in hours.

`0` is a **400**, not a synonym for `null`. A zero-hour window is an
immediate clearance wearing the delay's name — the mail saying
"this is happening, sign in to stop it" would arrive after the
factors were already gone. Someone who types `0` has misunderstood
the feature, and a 200 would leave them believing they had a safety
window.

Bounded above by 720 — thirty days,
past which the delay stops being a safety window and becomes a
refusal wearing a countdown's clothes.

Unlike the quota fields below, this is **not** platform-only. It is
the tenant's own security posture, the same class of decision as
`mfa_policy`, and the tenant is who bears it.

Audited as `mfa.self_recovery_changed` (warning) in every direction,
including off — turning it off strands anybody already counting
down.

passkey_attestation.description:
Turn hardware-key pinning on or off. Read `passkey_attestation` in
`TenantDetail` before setting this — it excludes every synchronised
authenticator, which for most consumer tenants is most of their users.

**`required` is a 409 while the tenant has no attestation CA.** That state
fails every registration, so it is refused rather than created: add a CA at
`POST /api/v1/tenants/{tenant_id}/passkey-attestation/cas` first.

A value outside the enum is a **400**, not a silent fallback. The stored
value is parsed leniently on read — an unrecognised one reads as `none`, so
a corrupt setting cannot lock a tenant's users out — but that reasoning does
not extend to a value somebody just typed here, where answering 200 to
`"require"` would leave a tenant unprotected and its operator convinced
otherwise.

Audited as `passkey.attestation_changed` (warning) in both directions.

max_self_registered_clients.description:
This tenant's cap on RFC 7591 self-registered clients.
**Three-state, and the states are the point**:

* field **absent** → leave the override alone;
* field present as **`null`** → clear the override, restoring the
  deployment default;
* an **integer ≥ 0** → set it; `0` means "accept no new ones".

A merely optional field cannot tell absent from `null`, and the
difference is the whole point of a nullable override.

**Platform token only**, checked when this field is sent rather than
for every PATCH — a
tenant-scoped key can legitimately PATCH its own tenant, so without
this "every customer could raise its own ceiling and the control
would be advisory". Sending the field at all as a tenant key is 403
`forbidden`, including when its value is `null`.

A negative value is 400 `invalid_request`, and so is one past
2147483647, the column's limit — both refused before anything in the
request is written. Not audited.

max_members.description:
**Platform token only.** A seat cap a customer can raise is not a cap,
so a tenant-scoped key is refused here even though it may PATCH its own
tenant for `mfa_policy`.

`null` clears the limit. The floor is 1, not 0: a tenant with no members
has nobody who can administer it and nobody who can raise the cap, and
the database refuses it too. The ceiling is 2147483647, the column's
limit; past it is a 400 too. Both are refused before anything in the
request is written.

A grant that would exceed the cap is refused, and the console shows a
message naming the cap rather than a generic error.

mfa_email_factor_enabled.description: Turns the email second factor on or off for this tenant. Off by default. Know what it buys: the address it mails a code to is the address password recovery writes to, so against somebody holding the mailbox it adds nothing — what it defends is a leaked password database, credential stuffing, and passwords reused elsewhere, which is most of what happens to most accounts. Audited as `tenant.mfa_email_factor_changed`.

account_recovery_codes_enabled.description: Turns saved account-recovery codes on or off for this tenant. Off by default. A code is offered only to an account with a password and no confirmed address; it sets a new password and never gets past a second factor. Turning it off withdraws no code — it stops every one being accepted until it is turned on again. Audited as `tenant.account_recovery_codes_changed`.

password_signup_enabled.description: Turns the hosted sign-up page on or off for this tenant: whether a person may make their own account here with an address and a password. Off by default. Turning it off removes no account. Audited as `tenant.password_signup_changed`.

social_signup_enabled.description: Turns account-making by social sign-in on or off for this tenant. Off, a first sign-in through a social connection that matches no account is refused, and a person who already has an account still signs in. Off by default for a new tenant. Audited as `tenant.social_signup_changed`.

plan_override.description: **Platform token only.** Puts the tenant on a plan by hand (a comp, an agreement, a test tenant), or `null` to clear it and let the subscription decide. The billing provider never writes this, so an override survives every subscription change. Audited as `tenant.plan_override_set` (warning).

TenantsApiError.description: The uniform error shape. `error` and `message` are always present, and `detail` when a body could not be read.

error.description: Stable slug. Every value this group can emit is enumerated here.

message.description: Human-readable; not stable, and it interpolates values (scope names, every known scope, the challenge host).

detail.description: Only on a 400 whose `message` is "invalid JSON body": what about the body could not be read, as the parser reports it — the unknown field and the fields expected, the type that did not fit, a missing `Content-Type: application/json`. At most 300 characters, and it can quote what was sent. Not stable; for a person reading it, not for matching.

metric.description: Named rather than implied, so a second metric later cannot be mistaken for this one.

definition.description: The counting rule, restated in every response: distinct users who signed in **or refreshed a token**, per calendar month, UTC. Refreshes count because a user who never re-authenticates would otherwise register only in the month they last typed a password. Client-credentials refreshes have no resource owner and are not counted.

period.description:
First day of the month `active_users` describes.

Required and non-nullable, which this schema did not say for a while.
It is the period of the last element of `series`, so it is null
exactly when the series is empty — and the series cannot be empty:
`months` is clamped to 1–24 before the query, with `0` read as the
default of 12, and at least one row comes back for any month count of
1 or more. The document also
contradicted itself, marking this nullable while `series[].period` is
required and non-nullable for the identical value.

resets_at.description: When `active_users` starts again from zero: 00:00 UTC on the first day of the month after `period`, as an RFC 3339 timestamp (`2026-11-01T00:00:00Z`). The count follows the calendar month in UTC, not the subscription: a plan that renews on the 14th still counts from the 1st.

active_users.description: The current month. Identical to the last element of `series`.

series.description: Oldest first, with quiet months present as zero rather than omitted — a chart that skips an empty August draws a different shape from the truth.

soft_cap.description: The tenant's own monthly-active-user soft cap, as it set it, or null for none. Reported even when unset — "this tenant has no cap of its own" is an answer a billing screen needs, and an absent field would make it guess. The cap that announces is `effective_soft_cap`.

effective_soft_cap.description: The cap that announces `usage.soft_cap_exceeded`: `soft_cap` when the tenant set one, otherwise the plan's `included_active_users`. `null` when neither applies — no cap of its own on a deployment that does not enforce plans.

over_soft_cap.description: Whether `active_users` has passed `effective_soft_cap` — the cap the audit trail announces at, so the two cannot disagree. Computed here rather than left to the caller, because every caller would compute it and one of them would use `>=`. Always false when there is no cap.

included_active_users.description: How many monthly recurring users the plan includes. On FREE it is the number the plan promises (passing it denies nobody anything); on TEAM and BUSINESS it is where per-user overage billing begins. `null` where the tenant is not held to its plan (plans not enforced, or the platform's own tenant).

over_included.description: `active_users > included_active_users`, computed here so no caller writes `>=`. False when `included_active_users` is null.

UserCreateRequest.description: Unknown fields are refused, so a typo is a 400 rather than a silently ignored field on a call that mints a credential.

tenant_id.description: Required when using the platform token, which will not guess a tenant.

username.description: Trimmed; must not be empty. Unique within the tenant.

password.description: At least 12 characters. Hashed with Argon2id before storage and never returned.

email.description: Optional. Trimmed; an empty string is stored as null. Otherwise a bare address — at most 254 bytes once trimmed, no whitespace or control character, and an addr-spec with nothing around it: no display name, angle brackets, comment or list, and no quoted local part, at a domain name with a dot, not an IP address or other bracketed literal: the rule every endpoint that takes an address applies, because the account's mail all goes to it.

email_verified.description:
Whether you are vouching for the address. Defaults to `true`.

This decides whether a social sign-in bearing the same address later joins this account or creates its own. `true` is the compatible answer and the honest one for this endpoint: it takes `users:write`, so the caller is trusted by the tenant to create accounts, and the address they type is the one linking has always been allowed to match against.

Send `false` when you are relaying an address a stranger typed — a sign-up form of your own, an import of unverified data. Those accounts are not linkable until their owner confirms the address at `/account/email`.

Ignored without an `email`: there is nothing to vouch for.
What was actually recorded — `false` when no address was given, whatever was requested.

id.description: The `user_id` to pass to the two action endpoints below.

email.description: The key is always present and may be null.

UsersMfaStatus.description: The second-factor inventory in the user lookup.

totp.description:
TRUE ONLY for a CONFIRMED enrolment: "only a
confirmed enrollment counts". A user midway through
enrolling reads `false` here even though a pending secret exists. That
pending secret is nonetheless destroyed by the reset endpoint and
counted there as `pending`.

passkeys.description: Registered passkey count. Falls back to `0` if the count cannot be read.

recovery_codes_remaining.description: UNUSED recovery codes. Falls back to `0` on error.

email.description: A confirmed email second factor (codes mailed to the account's address). Falls back to `false` if it cannot be read.

sms.description: A verified SMS second factor (codes texted to an enrolled US or Canadian number). Falls back to `false` if it cannot be read.

UsersResetMfaRequest.description:
Unknown fields are refused. See the operation's requestBody note for what an
absent body and an unreadable one each produce.

tenant_id.description:
Required with the platform token — 400 otherwise, and this is checked
BEFORE `reason`. Must be the key's own tenant otherwise (403).

reason.description:
REQUIRED in effect, though not marked required. Absent,
`null`, `""` and any whitespace-only string are all equivalent and all
yield 400 `invalid_request`.
"Free text recorded in the audit trail. Required: an unexplained reset
is indistinguishable from an attack after the fact, and asking for one
sentence at the moment of the action is the cheapest way to keep the
trail worth reading".
CAPPED, but only on the way into the audit row: control characters are
stripped and the value truncated to the first 200 CHARACTERS there. The full untruncated
value is sent to the webhook. It is NOT echoed in this
endpoint's response — unlike `sessions/revoke`, which does echo it.

totp_removed.description: Whether a confirmed TOTP enrolment existed and was removed.

email_removed.description: Whether an email second factor was removed. The reset used to leave it in place.

sms_removed.description: Whether an SMS second factor (and any code in flight for it) was removed. Staged, unverified numbers count.

note.description:
One of exactly two sentences:
  * "this user had no second factors; nothing changed"
  * "the user can sign in with their primary credential; a required
    tenant policy will make them enrol again"
Present to "say plainly what the account now looks like, so an
operator is not left guessing whether the user can get in".
Note a discarded pending enrolment also counts as a change, so a user whose ONLY anomaly was a staged enrolment gets the second
sentence while the factor fields all read false/0.

UsersResetMfaResponse.x-fields-deliberately-absent:
`ResetSummary` carries two more facts this response does NOT expose
(mfa.rs):
  * `pending_discarded` — an abandoned enrolment destroyed by the reset.
    It reaches the audit detail as `pending=` (:987) and the webhook as
    `pending_enrolment_discarded` (:1011), but has no HTTP field. A caller
    reading only this body cannot distinguish a plain no-op from one that
    killed an attacker's staged secret — the exact case the field was
    added for (mfa.rs).
  * `sessions_revoked_at` — the instant every credential died. Present in
    the `sessions/revoke` response but not here, even though this endpoint
    always revokes too (mfa.rs).

UsersRevokeSessionsRequest.description:
Unknown fields are refused, and the body is handled as the MFA reset's
is.

tenant_id.description: Required with the platform token (checked before `reason`); must be the key's own tenant otherwise.

reason.description:
REQUIRED in effect. Absent, `null`, `""` and whitespace-only are all
400 `invalid_request` — "an unexplained eviction is indistinguishable
from an attack after the fact". Trimmed before use, echoed back
verbatim in the response, and written into the `sessions.revoked`
audit detail.

sessions_revoked_at.description:
RFC 3339.
Everything issued at or before this instant is dead.

reason.description: The trimmed reason, echoed back in full — the 200-character truncation applies only to the audit detail.

performed_by.description:
Names the CREDENTIAL, never a
person: "the server can attest to the credential used, not the person
holding it". A person asserted via `X-Proteles-Operator`
goes to the audit row, not here.

note.description:
Always the same sentence: "every session, refresh token, authorization code and device code issued before this instant is dead; access tokens already minted are refused at introspection and userinfo, but an API that only checks their signature accepts them until they expire". Present to "say the
residual rather than let 'revoked' imply more than it does".

WebhookAcknowledgeRequest.description: Every field optional, and the body itself is optional: absent or empty means every outstanding letter. A body that is present and cannot be read — malformed JSON, a wrong type, a content type other than JSON, or an unknown key — is a 400 `invalid_request` "invalid JSON body" and acknowledges nothing.

ids.description: "Omitted or empty means every outstanding one matching `webhook_id` — after a receiver's outage that is the actual intent, and acknowledging four hundred letters one call at a time is a good way to ensure nobody acknowledges any of them".

WebhookDeadLetter.description: An event whose delivery gave up — see `GET /api/v1/webhook/dead-letters`.

webhook_id.description: Null once the endpoint has been deleted. "The letter survives that on purpose" — such a letter can never be revived, only acknowledged or discarded.

endpoint_name.description: Snapshot taken at death, so "which receiver was this for" stays answerable after the endpoint is gone. `"deleted endpoint"` when the endpoint was already absent.

body.description: The payload that was never delivered, as a JSON *string* — frozen at enqueue time.

revived_at.description: Set while a revived copy is back in the queue; cleared if it dies again.

revivals.description: How many times this has been rescued and died again.

acknowledged_by.description: The credential that acknowledged it — `platform-token` or `tenant-api-key`.

outstanding.description: Tenant-wide, unfiltered by `webhook_id` and untruncated by `limit`. "This is the number an alarm watches".

outstanding_by_endpoint.description: Endpoint id (as a string key) → outstanding count. Counted in the database, not tallied from the page. Only endpoints that still exist appear; orphaned letters are inside `outstanding` with nothing to attribute them to.

retention_days.description: The deployment's `DEAD_LETTER_RETENTION_DAYS` (default 90, held to 0–36525). The configured policy, not a promise that a sweeper is running. `0` means acknowledged letters are kept indefinitely. Only *acknowledged* and *not revived* letters are ever purged.

webhook_name.description: Read from the endpoint, so null once the endpoint is gone.

event_id.description: The `id` inside the payload. "A receiver uses it to deduplicate, which it must: retries make this at-least-once, never exactly-once".

status.description: Only these two: a delivery that gives up leaves this listing for the dead-letter queue.

attempts.description: Incremented even when the receiver is unreachable, "so a permanently dead endpoint exhausts and stops rather than retrying forever".

last_status.description: The HTTP status the receiver last answered with, if it answered.

WebhookDiscardRequest.description: Unknown fields are refused: a 400 `invalid_request` "invalid JSON body", and nothing is done.

ids.description: "Required and non-empty: unlike acknowledge, an empty list is not 'everything'. Deleting a whole category is not a thing this API knows how to be asked for". Omitted is read as `[]` and is then refused with the same message as an explicit `[]`.

discarded.description: How many rows actually went. Smaller than `requested` when an id is not this tenant's or was already gone.

requested.description: How many ids were sent — reported so the shortfall is visible.

WebhookEndpoint.description: Returned by GET /api/v1/webhooks and GET /api/v1/webhooks/{id}. Every key is always present; the nullable ones are explicit `null`.

name.description: A label, so an operator with several can tell them apart.

events.description: Subscription is explicit rather than "everything": "adding a new event type later must not start sending a tenant data they never asked for".

max_deliveries_per_minute.description: "Reported as 0 rather than null so 'unlimited' is stated rather than looking like a missing field". A limit on *our* sending rate; nothing is dropped, a throttled delivery waits. A burst is capped at one minute's allowance — the rate itself.

disable_after_dead_letters.description: Outstanding dead letters tolerated before the endpoint is switched off automatically. `0` means never, "matching the rate field's spelling of 'unlimited'" — and 0 is also the *stored* spelling of never. Only failures the endpoint caused count toward it; ours never do.

disabled_reason.description: "Null on an enabled endpoint, and also on one switched off before this was recorded — 'disabled, and we do not know why' being the truth about those rather than something to guess at". An unrecognised stored value also reads as null rather than being forced into one of these.

disabled_by.description: The credential, not the human — `platform-token`, `tenant-api-key`, or `automatic` for the threshold.

WebhookEndpointCreate.description: The body of `POST /api/v1/webhooks`. Unknown fields are refused: a 400 `invalid_request` "invalid JSON body", and nothing is done.

tenant_id.description: Required with the platform token; must match the key's own tenant otherwise. Read from the body on this operation, not the query.

url.description: Must be `https` unless the deployment allows insecure destinations, must have a host, and must not name a private, loopback, link-local, CGNAT or cloud-metadata address — including via an IPv4-in-IPv6 encoding.

secret.description: The HMAC key the receiver verifies with. Required here. Minimum 16 characters — "it is the only thing separating our deliveries from anyone else's POST". Never returned by any read.

events.description: Required and non-empty. Omitted is read as `[]` and is then refused with the same message as an explicit `[]`.

enabled.description: Accepted and **ignored on create**. A new endpoint is always enabled.

max_deliveries_per_minute.description: Omitted → 60. `0` → unlimited. Negative → 400. Absent and `0` mean different things.

WebhookEndpointReplace.description: The body of `PUT /api/v1/webhooks/{id}`, the same shape as create's. A full replace: `secret` and `enabled` keep their stored values when omitted, `url` and `events` are required, and an omitted `name`, `max_deliveries_per_minute` or `disable_after_dead_letters` resets to its default rather than keeping what is stored. Unknown fields are refused: a 400 `invalid_request` "invalid JSON body", and nothing is done.

tenant_id.description: Read from the body on this operation, not the query.

secret.description: Omission preserves, as it does for `enabled`: absent keeps the stored secret, "so an update that only changes the URL does not require re-sending the secret". Supplied, it must still be ≥ 16 characters.

events.description: Required and non-empty, as on create.

enabled.description: Omitted keeps the stored value — absent means "leave it as it is", not "switch it on". A change of state is what gets audited, and it clears or sets the disable provenance.

max_deliveries_per_minute.description: **Omitted resets to 60**, not "keep", exactly as on create.

WebhookEndpointWriteResult.description: What POST /api/v1/webhooks (201) and PUT /api/v1/webhooks/{id} (200) return. It echoes the resolved request rather than re-reading the row, so — unlike `WebhookEndpoint` — it has no `disabled_reason` / `disabled_at` / `disabled_by`.

enabled.description: Always `true` on create, whatever the request said. On replace, the resolved value (request `enabled`, or the stored one if omitted).

check.description: Which check: `active`, `refresh_token`, `openid`, `redirect_uris`, `post_logout_redirect_uris` or `backchannel_logout`. A check may report more than one finding (`redirect_uris` reports one per address it has something to say about).

level.description: `ok`: as it should be. `info`: worth knowing, nothing breaks. `warning`: works, probably not as meant. `problem`: will fail for somebody.

message.description: The finding, in a sentence for a person.

WebhookEventName.description: The supported event names. "Small on purpose — each entry is a promise about payload shape that someone else's code will depend on." An unknown name is refused at write time rather than stored, because "a typo would otherwise look configured and silently never fire".

WebhookReplayRequest.description: Every field optional, and the body itself is optional: absent or empty means all the defaults. A body that is present and cannot be read — malformed JSON, a wrong type, a content type other than JSON, or an unknown key — is a 400 `invalid_request` "invalid JSON body" and replays nothing.

webhook_id.description: "Confine the replay to one endpoint. After a single receiver's outage that is what an operator wants — not everyone else's deliveries re-sent too." Omitted means all.

status.description: `exhausted` revives dead letters — "the one that matters — the events lost while an endpoint was down". `delivered` re-sends from the live queue, "for a receiver that accepted events and then lost them". Anything else is a 400; `pending` in particular is refused because it is queued already.

since.description: RFC 3339. "Only those created at or after this … time, so an operator can name the outage window rather than replaying all history". Omitted means all history.

ids.description: Exactly these dead letters. "of four hundred lost events an operator may judge twelve worth another attempt … 'all of them' is not a decision anyone wants to be pushed into". Omitted or empty means "everything matching the filters". Only legal with `status: exhausted`.

more_may_remain.description: True when exactly 500 — the per-call cap — were requeued. "Say plainly whether there is more, rather than leaving a caller to guess why their backlog did not clear".

ServiceAccountCreateRequest.description: Unknown fields are refused: a 400 `invalid_request` "invalid JSON body", and nothing is done.

tenant_id.description:
OMITTED + platform token -> 400 `invalid_request`.
OMITTED + tenant key -> the key's own tenant.
PRESENT + tenant key naming a different tenant -> 403 `forbidden`.

name.description:
What the principal is called. It shares the username namespace, because a
service account IS a user rather than a separate kind of record — so it
collides with human usernames in the same tenant, and a name
already taken here is a 409.

Trimmed; empty or whitespace-only -> 400 `invalid_request`, "name is
required".

id.description:
The principal id. This is what goes in `service_account_id` when binding a
client to it — there is no lookup-by-name, so record it.

kind.description:
Always `service`. It is created with NO PASSWORD, which is
the server's existing marker for "cannot authenticate by password", and
the database enforces that with a constraint. A service account cannot
be made to sign in as a person later by setting a password on it.

ServiceAccountBindRequest.description: Unknown fields are refused: a 400 `invalid_request` "invalid JSON body", and nothing is done. That matters more here than most: an absent `service_account_id` unbinds, so a misspelling of it used to be a 200 that left the client unbound, detaching whatever principal it had.

tenant_id.description: Required when using the platform token; see `POST /api/v1/apps`.

service_account_id.description:
The principal this client acts as. ABSENT and `null` are IDENTICAL and both
UNBIND, returning the client to acting as itself — so an empty body clears
the binding. That is deliberate: the field is the whole state, and PUT
replaces state.

Must name a service account IN THIS TENANT. A human user's id, or a
principal from another tenant, is a 400.

ServiceAccountBound.description:
The 200 body of `PUT /api/v1/apps/{client_id}/service-account` — the binding
as it now stands, so the caller need not re-read to confirm.

total.description: Every match, not the page. Without it a full page is indistinguishable from the last page.

email.description: Where the link goes, and the address the owner's account is created with. Trimmed, then checked for shape only, by the rule every endpoint that takes an address applies: at most 254 bytes, an `@`, no whitespace or control character, and a bare address (an addr-spec, with no display name, angle brackets or comment, and no quoted local part, at a domain name with a dot, not an IP address or other bracketed literal), so the address mailed is the address the account is given. The address is proved by the mail arriving. On `DELETE` it is only looked up, not held to this rule: trimmed, not blank and free of control characters, and matched case-insensitively against what was sent, so an invitation sent before the rule was tightened can still be withdrawn.

delivered.description: Whether the deployment's relay accepted the mail. `false` does not mean the invitation failed — it exists and its link works — so send it again once the relay is fixed; the new link replaces this one.

replaced.description: The addresses of the platform's other live owner invitations in this workspace, withdrawn by this one: their links no longer work. Usually empty; one entry when the previous invitation went to another address.

withdrawn.description: `true` when a live invitation from the platform was withdrawn; `false` when there was none — accepted, expired, never sent, or sent by somebody else.

tenant_id.description: Required for the platform token; ignored by a tenant key, which can only name its own.

email.description: Where the link goes, and the address the account is created with. Trimmed, then checked for shape only: a bare address — at most 254 bytes once trimmed, no whitespace or control character, and an addr-spec with nothing around it: no display name, angle brackets, comment or list, and no quoted local part, at a domain name with a dot, not an IP address or other bracketed literal — the rule every endpoint that takes an address applies, so the address mailed is the address the account is given. The address is proved by the mail arriving.

client_id.description: OPTIONAL. The app to return the invitee to (issue #2): a `client_id` of this tenant, switched on, whose registration carries an `initiate_login_uri`. On accepting, a new account is signed in — through enrolment or a challenge first where the workspace requires a second factor — and the browser is sent to that URI with `iss` set to the workspace's issuer and nothing else; the app starts its ordinary sign-in there, which the new session answers. An address that already had an account is sent to the app without a session, and signs in there as usual. The URI is read from the app when the invitation is accepted, so one changed or removed in between is honoured as it is then; an app deleted, switched off or without one by then ends the acceptance on the sign-in page, as an invitation with no `client_id` does. ABSENT: exactly that. The link is on the host the app signs in at, since that is where accepting signs the person in and which issuer `iss` names: the workspace's own address, `<slug>.<base host>`, or for the default workspace the base host itself.

expires_at.description: 72 hours out. Longer than a password reset deliberately: a reset is sent to somebody at their keyboard asking for it, and an invitation arrives unannounced and may sit until Monday.

SamlServiceProvider.description:
A service provider this tenant may sign users into, with Proteles as the identity provider.

`acs_urls` is an allowlist: an AuthnRequest naming a destination not byte-equal to one of these is refused, never delivered to the closest match.

name.description: The tenant-visible name. Never sent anywhere.

sp_entity_id.description: Stored and compared byte for byte; no normalisation of any kind.

acs_urls.description: Absolute https, exact byte equality at use. The order means nothing: an AuthnRequest carrying an AssertionConsumerServiceIndex is refused, and the default is default_acs_url.

default_acs_url.description: Where an AuthnRequest that names no destination is answered. Always one of acs_urls, byte for byte.

request_signing_certificate_pem.description: Verifies a signed AuthnRequest from this SP, and when it is set every request must be signed. Null means this SP does not sign its requests: a signed request from it cannot be checked and is refused, so an SP that signs must have its certificate registered. It is never a fallback for one that fails verification.

enabled.description: Off until an administrator turns it on. A disabled registration answers as a missing one.

enrol_on_first_sign_in.description: Whether this application may be sent an identifier for somebody it has never seen — the question `<NameIDPolicy AllowCreate>` asks, answered here for the requests that do not ask it, which is most of them. An explicit `AllowCreate="false"` in a request is still honoured. Not about *which* users may reach the application, only about minting the identifier the assertion carries.

slo_url.description: Where this service provider receives front-channel single-logout messages, over the HTTP-POST binding. Validated exactly as `acs_urls` are: absolute https, no wildcards, and never an address on this deployment. Null means this registration does not take part in single logout.

single_logout.description: Whether this application can take part in single logout, derived from `slo_url` and `request_signing_certificate_pem`. `takes_part`: its own logout requests are honoured, and it is told when another SAML application signs the person out here. `no_logout_endpoint`: its own requests are honoured, but it is never told when another application signs the person out, so that logout is answered `PartialLogout`. `no_certificate`: its logout requests are refused and its answers cannot be verified, so a logout started elsewhere passes it over. `no_logout_endpoint_or_certificate`: neither — it cannot start a logout here and is never told of one. Signing out at this server itself tells no SAML application.

open_to_every_tenant_user.description: Whether every user of this tenant may be asserted to this registration. False — the default — means only the users listed at /assignments may. The permissive answer is a flag an administrator sets deliberately, so it is never inferred and never defaulted to true.

SamlServiceProviderRequest.description: Whole replacement; there is no partial update, because a partial update of an allowlist is a way to add a destination without stating the whole set you meant to allow.

tenant_id.description: Platform tokens only; a tenant key naming another tenant is refused.

sp_entity_id.description: An absolute URI. Leading or trailing whitespace is refused rather than trimmed.

acs_urls.description: Each must be an absolute https URL with no userinfo, fragment, query, dot segment, percent-encoded separator, backslash or whitespace, and must survive its own parser unchanged. Wildcards and patterns are refused rather than stored literally. Duplicates are refused.

default_acs_url.description: Where an AuthnRequest that names no destination is answered. Must be one of acs_urls, exactly as written there. Required when acs_urls names more than one destination, because the list's order does not decide it; with one destination it may be omitted and means that one. A replacement must state it again.

request_signing_certificate_pem.description: The SP's request-signing certificate (PEM). Set it for an SP that signs its AuthnRequests: with it, unsigned requests are refused; without it, signed ones are, because they cannot be checked.

name_id_format.description: Defaults to persistent, the only format a new registration may name until the identity provider issues the others; a replacement keeps the registration's own.

enrol_on_first_sign_in.description: Whether this application may be sent an identifier for somebody it has never seen — the question `<NameIDPolicy AllowCreate>` asks, answered here for the requests that do not ask it, which is most of them. Absent means true: a registration that refused its own first sign-in would be met as a broken deployment rather than as a policy.

slo_url.description: Where this service provider receives front-channel single-logout messages, over the HTTP-POST binding. SamlIdpKey.description:
One of this tenant's SAML identity-provider signing keys.

The private half is never present, in any state, on any endpoint. Four states rather than a boolean, because a planned rotation needs published-but-not-yet-signing and a compromise needs revoked-and-never-again.

kid.description: Per tenant, never global. Two tenants may hold the same kid; they are different keys.

state.description: published: in metadata, signing nothing. signing: what signs today, exactly one per tenant. retired: no longer signing, still published until the overlap has passed. revoked: out of metadata at once and never back.

certificate_pem.description: The self-signed certificate. Public; served unauthenticated at the metadata endpoint.

certificate_sha256.description: SHA-256 of the certificate DER, lowercase hex — what an administrator confirms out of band.

not_after.description: Jittered per tenant at mint, so a bulk onboarding does not give a thousand customers the same morning to fail on.

signing_refused_from.description: When the signer stops using this key: a day before `not_after`. After this the tenant cannot sign with it.

rotation_warning_from.description: When the expiry warning starts: `not_after` less the rotation overlap, the refusal day and a week, and never less than thirty days before `not_after`, so a rotation started then can finish. retired_at.description: Null until a successor is promoted. The overlap is measured from here.

created_at.description: When access was granted. A repeat of a grant already made does not move it.

WebhookTenantIdRequired.description: `invalid_request`. A platform token must name the tenant explicitly; only a tenant API key may leave it out, because that key already is one.

WebhookUnauthorized.description: `unauthorized`. No bearer token, or one this deployment does not know. Answered identically for an absent and an invalid credential.

WebhookForbidden.description: `forbidden` or `insufficient_scope`. The credential is valid and does not carry what this route needs — a tenant key naming another tenant, or a restricted key without the scope.

WebhookManagementDisabled.description: `not_found`. The management API is not enabled on this deployment. A 404 rather than a 403, so an unconfigured deployment does not advertise a surface it does not serve.

WebhookServerError.description: `server_error`. Deliberately opaque: the reason is in the server's log with a correlation id, never in the body.

TenantsBadPathParam.description: `invalid_request`. A path parameter is not the shape this route needs — most often a tenant id that is not a UUID.

TenantsUnauthorized.description: `unauthorized`. No bearer token, or one this deployment does not know.

TenantsForbiddenOrScope.description: `forbidden` or `insufficient_scope`. Valid credential, insufficient authority — a tenant key naming another tenant, or a restricted key without the scope this route requires.

TenantsDomainsForbiddenOrScope.description: `forbidden` or `insufficient_scope`. As above, and on these routes the scope in question is `domains:write`.

TenantsManagementDisabled.description: `not_found`. The management API is not enabled on this deployment.

TenantsServerError.description: `server_error`. Opaque by design; the reason is in the log under a correlation id.

RateLimited.description:
`rate_limited` — default 300/min (`RATE_LIMIT_MANAGEMENT_PER_MIN`).

Every operation in this document can return this. The limiter matches `/api/v1/` by prefix, not from a list of routes, so metering is the default for this API and a new operation is throttled the day it ships.

The bucket is keyed on the caller's network, not on the API key: two keys behind one address share a budget, and the same key from two addresses gets two. Retry after the seconds named in `Retry-After`.

Retry-After.description: Whole seconds until the bucket refills. Always present on a 429 from this API; the server sets it on every rate-limited response.

RateLimitedUserAction.description:
`rate_limited` — default **10/min** (`RATE_LIMIT_USER_ACTION_PER_MIN`), thirty times tighter than the rest of this API.

The two operations that act on a user's credentials — clearing their second factors, ending every session they hold — are metered separately from everything else. Scopes decide whether a key may do this at all; this decides how fast. A key legitimately holding `users:reset_mfa` should not be able to disarm a tenant account by account as fast as the network allows.

It is a separate budget, not a share of the one the rest of this API draws on: spending either buys no progress against the other. Bulk work against these two operations needs pacing that the rest of the API does not.

Retry-After.description: Whole seconds until the bucket refills. Always present on a 429 from this API; the server sets it on every rate-limited response.

Unauthorized.description:
`unauthorized` — no bearer token, or one the server will not accept.

Every operation in this document can return this. Authentication is not a property of individual routes here: every operation authenticates the same way, before it reads its path, query string or body, and refuses in two cases — no `Authorization: Bearer` header at all ("a bearer token is required"), or a key that does not resolve ("invalid or revoked API key").

A revoked key is indistinguishable from a never-valid one, deliberately. Retrying does not help; mint a new key.

Forbidden.description:
`insufficient_scope` or `forbidden` — the key authenticated, and is not allowed to do this. Branch on `error`; `message` is a sentence for people and is not stable.

Every operation in this document can return this, for one of these causes:

- **`insufficient_scope`: scope.** The key does not hold the scope this operation requires. A key minted with no scopes at all passes every held-to-what-you-declare check but no strict one (see `TenantApiKeyScope`); one minted with any scope is restricted to exactly those.
- **`forbidden`: another tenant.** The key tried to act on a tenant other than its own. Only the platform token may name an arbitrary `tenant_id`; a tenant key naming somebody else's is refused here rather than silently rescoped.
- **`forbidden`: platform token only.** The operation takes no tenant key, whatever its scopes: creating, listing, exporting, deleting or changing the status of tenants, and inviting a tenant's owner; minting, listing, rotating or revoking API keys; reading or setting the per-tenant SAML switches; fleet health; and the quota fields of the tenant PATCH.
- **`owner_unconfirmed`: `POST /users/invite` from a tenant self-service sign-up made**, none of whose owners has confirmed their email address.
- **`forbidden`: a refusal of the operation's own**, described with it: deleting the default tenant; and registering or replacing a SAML service provider, assigning a user to one, or minting an identity-provider signing key while the platform has not enabled the tenant as a SAML identity provider or the tenant is not active.

Operations do not all run their checks in the same order, so a request that fails two of them may get either slug. Retrying unchanged does not help: each cause needs a different key, a different request, or an operator's change.

PasswordPoolBusy.description: `temporarily_unavailable` — the server's password-hashing pool (Argon2id) had no room in its queue, so the password or client secret was not hashed and nothing was written. Nothing about the request was wrong: send it again after `Retry-After`. The queue is shared with every other password check on the replica, sign-ins included, so a flood of those fills it too. Each one is counted in `proteles_password_hash_busy_total`.

Retry-After.description: Whole seconds before retrying. Always 1: a place in the queue frees each time one hash finishes.

TenantIdQuery.name: tenant_id
TenantIdQuery.description: Which tenant to act on. **Required with the platform token**, which belongs to no tenant and so cannot infer one; refused if it names a tenant other than a tenant API key's own, since that key already is one.

TenantsTenantId.name: tenant_id
TenantsTenantId.description: The tenant this route acts on. A value that is not a UUID is `invalid_request`, not `not_found` — the path is malformed rather than naming something absent.

TenantsDomainPath.name: domain
TenantsDomainPath.description: The claimed hostname, as stored: trimmed, lowercased, with no trailing dot. Sending the form a user typed rather than the normalised one is the usual reason a claim cannot be found.

TenantsAssertedOperator.name: X-Proteles-Operator
TenantsAssertedOperator.description: The human a platform caller says is at the keyboard, recorded beside the credential in the audit row as `asserted_operator=`. **Nothing verifies it** — the management API authenticates a credential, not a person — which is why the key says `asserted_` and why it is recorded beside `by=` rather than instead of it. Ignored, with a warning logged, when sent with a tenant API key.
